Madam Speaker, I rise today to present a number of petitions from constituents in my riding. These particular constituents reside in the communities of Lumby, Salmon Arm, Sicamous and Enderby.
These petitioners are calling upon the government to reconsider its decision to force the provinces to either increase funding for the RCMP, in many cases far greater than the municipalities can afford, or to decrease services and close detachments.
We recognize that a decision has been made recently in this regard.
These petitioners had signed these beforehand, but I think the petitioners are still relevant in presenting their case that RCMP services should be maintained at their current level, with the current levels of funding by the federal government.
On behalf of these petitioners, I present these to the House today.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise under Standing Order 36 to present a petition signed by quite a number of my constituents in the riding of Timmins-Chapleau, and in particular in South Porcupine.
The petitioners are calling on Parliament to support the maintenance of rural post offices and postal services. They also call on Parliament to reject the Conservative agenda to cut back and close these post offices.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to present to the House a petition from people in the riding of Perth- Wellington-Waterloo, the communities of Stratford, Mitchell and Shakespeare.
The petitioners consider the Income Tax Act discriminatory against the people who choose to stay home and look after their children as compared to buying child care services.
They believe the credits and allowances make it more advantageous for people with families to live together in an unmarried rather than a married state. They believe the system is cumbersome.
The petitioners pray that the House will amend the Income Tax Act to make it fair and equitable for all family arrangements that are available.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure today to present two petitions on behalf of my constituents, pursuant to Standing Order 36.
The first petition deals with the goods and services tax, the tax that was supposed to be so simple and so effective. It was supposed to be revenue neutral.
My constituents from the communities of Rainy River, Emo, and Fort Frances ask that this particular tax be rescinded. They humbly petition this place, this House of Parliament, to rescind the goods and services tax and find a simple, fair and efficient means to levy taxes in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I also have a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36 which deals with the government's large tax increases and its belief that in order to get its house in order, it would discriminate against working men and women in this country by freezing their wages in the public sector, and by doing so, enabling itself to get out of the mess that it put itself in.
Again, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject the imposition of wage controls and reaffirm support for free collective bargaining in this country for Canadian workers.
June 6, 1991

Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I have a petition today signed by the residents of Saskatchewan, some from my riding and some neighbouring my riding in the communities of Debden and Big River, rural Saskatoon and Shelbrooke.
The petitioners state that 12,000 Canadian members of our merchant navy served their country during the Second World War, 1,259 of whom died in combat.
The petitioners state that the United States and the United Kingdom have recognized that merchant seamen are veterans, and they state that approximately 3,500 Canadians served in dangerous waters during the last war and seek what they sought since the end of the war: equal recognition, entitlement and benefits, a position supported by the Royal Canadian Legion.
These petitioners call upon Parliament to pass legislation that would confer veteran status to those who served in Canada's merchant navy during the Second World War.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to have this opportunity to speak on Bill C-17 which amends Part III of the Criminal Code dealing with firearms and other weapons.
All Canadians are aware of the need for changes to Canada's gun control system. This government is committed to the reduction of crime, and effective gun control measures are an important part of Canada's criminal law. The time is right for this House to respond to the concerns of all Canadians. Four out of five Canadians support stronger gun control and with good reason. Most important, Canadians are becoming increasingly concerned about the increase of firearms violence.
The ownership of firearms of all kinds is increasing and Canadian police forces are becoming increasingly concerned about the frequency with which they are being used in crimes of all kinds, ranging from domestic violence to armed robbery and even mass murder.

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
There is some misunderstanding about the nature of the issue and the nature of firearms related violence or homicides with respect to urban and rural Canadians. In fact, public opinion polls show that the concern for stronger gun control is shared by Canadians who live in communities of less than 10,000 people as much as by Canadians who live in large urban centres.
In addition, according to the Canadian justice statistics, homicide rates caused by firearms are just as high per capita in small communities under 10,000 as in large communities. In fact, they are greater per capita in communities under 10,000 than in communities of greater than 500,000 and are only exceeded by communities from 100,000 to 250,000.
The concern for firearms related homicides and the concern to have effective and sensible gun control is a concern that is shared by Canadians all across this country in communities of all sizes in urban and rural areas.
The existing gun control law has not changed significantly since January 1, 1978 and changes are needed. This government is being asked to take strong and effective measures to control firearms. As the hon. members of this House are aware, on June 26, 1990, I introduced Bill C-80 which contained a number of new gun control proposals. This bill was studied by a special committee of members of this House which produced a report containing a total of 32 recommendations for changes in the legislation.
Many of these recommendations make a contribution to stronger controls and have been taken into account in revising the legislation. Bill C-17 is the government's response to the special committee report.
I am grateful for the hard work and support of the committee members, and I would like to thank them for their contribution to the new legislation.

Madam Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-80 was to provide better protection for all Canadians against firearms violence, while avoiding undue or unnecessary interference in the activities of Canadians who use guns legally, responsibly, and safely.
The legislation now before this House contains a number of modifications to Bill C-80, but the fundamental purpose remains the same. I believe that the modifications that have been made contribute to the achievement of a safer, more balanced, and more effective gun control system.
The measures contained in this Bill will improve Canada's gun control system in many different ways. Taken together, they comprises a package that will help to ensure that those who should not have guns do not have guns.
They will take the wrong guns out of all hands, and all guns out of the wrong hands. They will result in better screening of gun buyers, and they will limit access to the most dangerous types of firearms. They will reduce the accidental misuse of guns. They will encourage the responsible ownership and use of guns by all Canadians. They will help to keep firearms out of the hands of those who should not have them or who might use them for criminal purposes. And finally, they will increase deterrence for those who may use guns criminally or negligently.
I believe that these measures, with your strong support, will help alleviate the personal sense of fear and vulnerability that many people experience in today's society.

Under the new proposals deterrence of firearms crime will be increased by raising the maximum sentences for some of the offences created by the gun control law. Witnesses who appeared before the Reimer committee, the special committee of the House of Commons, including police and customs officers, suggested that one major source of illegal firearms is illegal imports. To respond to this, the maximum sentences for importing, possessing or selling prohibited weapons will all increase from five to ten years.
Another major concern expressed by the police community has been the association of firearms with specific areas of criminal activity. In response to this, the legislation will also extend the use of prohibition orders to offences of drug trafficking as a bail condition and upon conviction.
To supplement this, the sentence for possessing any firearm while under a court prohibition order will also increase from five to ten years.
June 6, 1991

Canadians are very concerned about problems of violence against women and violence in domestic situations, and 1 share these concerns. All members of this House will realize that this is not just a gun control problem, but clearly firearms are a factor in many situations and the gun control law must recognize this. The presence of firearms in many homes raises grave concerns when domestic disputes occur. Too many of the domestic homicides that occur in Canada each year involve a firearm: easy access to a gun in a domestic dispute is an invitation to tragedy.
An important difference between gun control and other elements of Canada's criminal law and justice system is that gun control seeks to prevent as well as deter firearms incidents. Several elements of this bill will address concerns about domestic violence by helping the justice system to remove guns from potentially violent situations at the earliest possible time.
The present law provides for mandatory or discretionary firearms prohibition orders where there is a conviction for a violent offence. The new legislation will require the courts to consider firearms prohibition orders before conviction in some cases. When an accused person has been charged with an offence in which violence was used, threatened, or attempted, the court will be required to consider whether to make prohibition or other conditions a part of the bail order if the safety of any person might be jeopardized by not doing so.
A similar process will apply to peace bond applications which often arise during domestic disputes. This measure is intended to encourage the police and the courts to remove firearms from potentially violent situations before tragedy can occur. Where a person is convicted of a violent offence that carries a maximum sentence of 10 years or more, a five-year firearms prohibition order is already mandatory. This legislation will increase the prohibition to 10 years, with a lifetime prohibition for any repeat offence. Where the sentence available is less than 10 years, the courts currently have the discretion to prohibit for up to five years; but there are concerns that prohibitions are underused.
Under the proposed amendments the court will retain this discretion but will be required by law to consider prohibition even where the matter is not raised by counsel.
Government Orders
Under the present law police may also make an application to a court where they have reasonable grounds to believe that allowing a person to keep a firearm or acquisition certificate would endanger the safety of any person. This provision is an important one for domestic violent situations and will be kept unchanged.
I will be asking my provincial counterparts to encourage police officers across Canada to use it wherever possible to remove firearms from dangerous situations before they can cause harm.
Taken in combination, I believe that these changes should substantially increase the use of firearms prohibitions as a means of removing firearms from potentially dangerous situations, many of them domestic disputes, both before and after a conviction for any offence.
I might add that certainly one of the concerns that has been raised by lawful and responsible firearms users in Canada is the notion that the law must be enforced adequately and must address the criminal and misuse of firearms. I think that message was very well received and I think that these additions to the legislation that came as a result of the consultation surrounding Bill C-80 strengthen it and really make a significant and helpful addition to the over all legislative framework.
For those who are concerned that the law is not enforced strictly enough with respect to firearms offences, two other approaches I wish to take, which are not inherent in the legislation are, first of all, to draft prosecutorial guidelines for my own prosecutors in the territories. I am the prosecutor for the criminal law only in the territories of Canada. I think the public would like to ensure that these offences are dealt with seriously and that Crown counsel does not plea bargain away such offences. I will provide my own guidelines for consultation with my provincial counterparts in September when we meet to encourage them to perhaps develop the same ones.
In addition, I have had discussions with the Director of the Canadian Judicial Centre about the possibility in the course of the judicial education programs provided to judges to provide some component that would sensitize members of our judiciary to the seriousness with which Canadians view offences related to firearms and their concern that these laws be carefully enforced. I have had

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
a very positive response to that. It is a broadly based initiative to try and ensure that the misuse of firearms is the major focus of our criminal activity.

Madam Speaker, the proposed legislation also contains a number of improvements to the screening system for those who request permission to acquire firearms. The firearms acquisition certificate system is at the heart of Canadian gun control.
By controlling the acquisition certificate, we insure that anyone who wants to obtain a gun must first be screened. Members will recall that this certificate is necessary to acquire a gun in any fashion, whether by purchase, gift, or loan.
The system only requires that those who want to keep a FAC be re-screened every five years to be sure that they are still suitable.
The screening system is a key element of our gun control proposals, and the legislation I have placed before this House contains many proposed changes to it. It will require all applicants to furnish two personal references who can assist those conducting the screening check. It will require a minimum 28 day waiting period during which that check will be carried out.
To prevent use by unauthorized persons, it will require the new FAC document to include a photograh of the holder. Finally, it will require FAC applicants to pass a firearms safety course or test.

Many concerns have been raised about the safety training requirement, especially on behalf of those Canadians for whom such a requirement might present an unnecessary or undue hardship. The new proposals will authorize local firearms officers who accept an FAC application to certify competence and knowledge without a formal test.
Regulations will be enacted to guide this discretion and to ensure that the exception is applied fairly and consistently. I anticipate that it may be used where the applicant can provide some other evidence of competence or where he or she is not able to complete a formal written examination.
It is difficult in this enormous country of ours with enormous regional variations to legislate fairly for all Canadians. We have to recognize that we have many Canadians who live in very remote areas. We have many Canadians who, unfortunately, are not literate and it is important to ensure that the standard is met but at the same time that the implementation is sufficiently flexible so as not to exclude Canadians who would otherwise be able to establish their competence.
A national safety education program is now being developed in consultation with my advisory council and provincial authorities. This provision will be proclaimed in force as soon as it can be implemented.
Concerns have also been raised about the possible liability of those who act as references. It has been suggested that the possibility of being held responsible for the applicant's use of firearms would effectively deter most potential references. It has also been suggested that the fear of liability might deter references from being candid about the applicant's suitability.
To address this problem, the law will make clear that a reference cannot be held civilly or criminally liable unless there has been a deliberate attempt to mislead the police, either by providing false information or deliberately failing to reveal significant information when it is requested.
I want to make it absolutely clear that references are only expected to assist the authorities to ensure that only those who do not represent a danger to the safety of themselves or anyone else are given access to firearms. Provided this basic standard is met, there will be no liability of any kind.
Concerns have also been raised that young people have access to firearms with too few restrictions. The new legislation will require FAC applicants between 16 and 18 years of age to obtain parental consent.

In many areas of Canada, the use of firearms by young persons is an important, and even an essential part of daily life. The law must provide for this, but it must also be sure that young persons are subject to appropriate supervision and controls.
In addition to requiring parental consent for a FAC application, the amendments will also give parents the option of consenting to a minors' permit up to age 18.
June 6, 1991

The minors' permit allows limited access to young people, and may have special conditions placed on it for supervision.

The fee charged for an acquisition certificate is currently $10. This is far below the cost of the screening process. The level is fixed by the statute and has not been changed since the last amendments were made in 1978. The new legislation will make it possible to set the fee by regulation which will allow for periodic adjustments to reflect changes in the cost of running the screening system.
There is no intention to use high fees to deter legitimate gun owners, but the taxpayers have been heavily subsidizing the current system. This government is committed to the principle of cost recovery and the firearms community agrees with us. Most of those who appeared on behalf of firearms groups before the special committee on gun control indicated that they believe that firearms owners should pay reasonable screening costs.

Madam Speaker, it has been suggested that the focus of Canada's gun control system be changed from screening FAC applicants to registering all firearms.
The present system requires a screening check before a person can acquire a gun of any kind. Those firearms that represent a greater risk are designated as restricted weapons, and these must be registered. The owners are recorded by the RCMP, and transfers must be reported.
The combination of these two systems allows us to focus the additional resources needed to register and track firearms on those types of guns associated with additional risk. Mandatory registration of all firearms would place much greater demands on the existing system.
It would require trained police officers to spend more time reviewing gun registrations, and less time screening the people who will possess the guns they are registered.
Registering firearms would tell us how many legal guns there are in Canada, Madam Speaker, but it would have little effect on their use in crime, or on the number of deaths and injuries caused by suicides and accidents each year.
Government Orders
In a time of fiscal restraint, this government prefers to concentrate the available gun control resources in those areas of the system that will provide real benefits to firearms users and to the public safety.
It has also been suggested that the expiry time for acquisition certificates be changed. Gun owners would like to see a longer term or easier renewals. Those on the other side of the issue would like to see FAC holders required to re-apply after only two years. The present five year period strikes an effective balance between rescreening too often and not often enough. To reduce this period to two or three years would increase screening costs without any benefit to public safety. To increase it beyond five years or to reduce the screening process would be to compromise public safety. This government will not compromise the safety of the Canadian public.
The amendments I am proposing have been carefully considered with a view to protecting all Canadians from firearms violence. They are also intended to regulate the possession and use of firearms in ways which make it possible for those who require them to obtain and use them with a minimum of unnecessary interference.
One way of doing this is to focus the regulatory system, as much as possible, on types of firearms associated with the greatest risk to public safety, and relatively few, if any, legitimate sporting uses.
There have been concerns raised about the increasing prevalence of military and high fire-power firearms in Canada since the law was last amended in 1978. Hon. members will recall that effective controls on fire-power were a major component of my earlier legislative proposals.
There are still serious concerns about these firearms that this House must address and they remain a key element of the current proposals. These firearms represent a much greater danger to the public than others and they are dealt with accordingly.
Those who own military or paramilitary firearms, fully automatic or converted fully automatic firearms face a much greater degree of restriction than others because their guns are much more dangerous. They are designed and intended for military, not sporting uses.

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
The laws dealing with these types of firearms are tough, and I make no apology for that. Many other countries have already prohibited machine guns and other military firearms and more will almost certainly do so in the future.
These amendments will make it clear that these guns have no place in Canada. In 1978 machine guns were made prohibited weapons. There are now large numbers of machine guns in Canada that have been converted to comply with the 1978 law but which still pose a serious threat. They cannot fire automatically but they have other characteristics such as military design and large magazine capacities which make them a problem. In many cases they can be reconverted to machine guns without great difficulty.
The amendments will allow those who now own such firearms to keep their guns, subject to restrictions on transfers to others. The only legitimate reason for wanting a converted machine gun is for a gun collection, and the amendments will only permit collectors who already own them to register them.
The amendments also include a definition of a genuine gun collector and will establish quite significant criteria and standards which must be met before someone can qualify for that category.
Before registering such a firearm, the police would ensure that it has been converted satisfactorily. I recognize that these individuals have obtained their guns legally and will now, in some cases, be unable to sell them. What the law will do is allow those who have these guns to keep them and to sell them to others who also already own similar ones. As these owners die or lose interest in their firearms, the guns will be forced out of circulation so that future generations of Canadians will not be faced with them.
These proposals are the best possible solution. I might add that this was the approach to grandfathering that was taken in 1978 with respect to automatic firearms and it has worked well, because in order to retain those firearms people have had to be brought into the system to be registered. They are known to the policing authorities and it gives us a much better handle on what firearms are there. Standards can be imposed for safe storage and safe handling and that, I think, has worked
very well with respect to those firearms. That is a closed class. Those firearms will go out of circulation as will the converted automatics.
These proposals take into account the property interests of present owners who obtained the guns legally, but most important, the interests of all Canadians which require that they be taken out of circulation entirely.

When I initially introduced Bill C-80, I indicated that it was also my intention to designate other types of military or paramilitary firearms as restricted or prohibited weapons.
This is intended to restrict the availability of the most dangerous firearms, and at the same time, underscore the traditional Canadian idea that firearms in society are more properly regarded as tools for hunting or sporting purposes and not weapons for personal or civil defence. These roles are very capably performed by the police and the armed forces of Canada, and should not serve as a justification for the private ownership of firearms.
It is not my intention, however, to restrict or prohibit every single type of firearm that has ever seen military service. I recognize that many older-style military guns have seen valuable service as hunting firearms.
What I am concerned about, and what the legislation seeks to control, are modem military firearms that contain high firepower, fast-firing mechanisms, large capacity cartridge magazines, and other characteristics that make them very dangerous weapons, and have little or no place in legitimate sporting activities. Where there are relatively few legitimate uses for these firearms, they would be prohibited altogether.
Where they are used for some forms of legitimate target shooting activity, they may be designated as restricted weapons, which would allow the activity to continue, but protect the public by registering and tracking the guns and their owners.

I want to reassure those who own obsolete military firearms such as the Lee Enfield that this proposal is intended to reduce access to the most modern semi-automatic military assault weapons.
June 6, 1991

Older models do not differ significantly from many common hunting rifles. There would be no point prohibiting or restricting these firearms and this government has no intention of doing so.
The Canadian Advisory Council on Firearms, which combines expertise and viewpoints from all sides of the firearms issue, is currently considering criteria for identifying military type firearms and will be reporting to me in the near future.
A number of the members of the advisory council, as firearms users themselves, have already pointed out the sporting applications of older military surplus guns. While I cannot predict the criteria the council will put forward, I am sure that it will reflect the necessary balance.
I would also point out that the final decision will be that of the government. The council is advisory, but the final decision will be made by the government. Those regulations will have the opportunity to be reviewed by this House.
There are many similarities and differences between military and sporting firearms. In trying to identify military guns, the law will have to pay close attention to the differences. Those guns that are clearly of a military nature will be dealt with as I have explained.
The most critical difference is the capacity of the cartridge magazine. The addition of a large magazine can convert almost any ordinary semi-automatic hunting rifle into an assault weapon. This legislation will designate large capacity magazines to be prohibited weapons.
It will also allow the Governor in Council to specify the types of magazine that will be limited and the capacity limits to be applied.
Limiting the size of magazines will supplement the other measures by placing effective limits on the firepower of guns that are on the borderline between military and sporting applications.
The previous proposals would have placed controls on magazine capacity, and the same limitations will also be imposed under the legislation now before this House.
If these amendments become law, I will be developing regulations that will limit the capacity of magazines for semi-automatic handguns to 10 shots, and will limit the
Government Orders
capacity of magazines for centrefire semi-automatic rifles to five shots, exactly as I proposed in the context of Bill C-80.
The fire-power of non semi-automatics and rim-fire .22 calibre rifles does not represent a problem. Magazines for these firearms would not be limited at all.
I also recognize that there are those who engage in legitimate target shooting competitions which normally use magazines that would become prohibited under the proposal. Where involvement in such an activity is established, these persons will be permitted to retain their magazines for competitive purposes. The controls will be strict, however.
Competition activities must be sanctioned and those who take part will only be permitted to keep magazines that are required for suitable types of firearms and firearms which they actually own and possess.
I also recognize that many semi-automatic firearms cannot be used without the magazines designed for them. Collectors and other persons who have large magazines will be permitted to keep them provided that they are modified in an approved manner to reduce capacity to an acceptable limit. The regulations will be worded in such a way as to make this a practical option.
This is similar to the requirements in some provinces to limit semi-automatic hunting rifles to three shots under the terms of a hunting licence. In other words, the practice of blocking off some of the chambers in a magazine to comply with a legal limitation on a number of shots is well established already in Canadian society. We will try to establish standards of conversion that are both effective but also practical to implement.
The gun control system treats all handguns as restricted weapons, and requires that they be registered individually. The present system of permits for possession and use has proven effective at reducing handgun shootings, but it does create obstacles for legitimate shooters.
Some degree of inconvenience is inevitable, if gun control is to be effective at all, but I have attempted to remove unnecessary red tape wherever possible.

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
The bill will address some of the administrative concerns of handgun shooters by creating three new permits for restricted weapons.

The permit to carry, which is required to take a handgun to shoot at a range, will be expanded to allow more than one permit to be used for the same gun so that more than one shooter may share it. The holder of the second permit would be allowed to take the gun to a shooting range without having the registered owner present.
Competition organizers have raised concerns about the obstacles facing foreign shooters coming to Canada to take part in sanctioned competitions here. A new temporary carry permit will be created to allow these shooters to bring their handguns into Canada in order to attend sanctioned Canadian shooting competitions and to transport the guns to and from the point of entry.
A new temporary storage permit will also be created to allow a gun owner to store his or her handguns with another owner temporarily where it is unsafe or not practicable to store the gun at home, as is normally required. This will allow persons going on vacation, for example, to store their guns with a friend while they are away and is consistent with our emphasis on higher standards of safe storage.
As Canadian firearms owners are aware, a portion of the gun control system is enacted by a combination of regulations and Orders in Council made under the legislative authority of the Criminal Code. This combined approach makes for a better system for all concerned because it allows for flexibility and clarity which would not be possible using the statute alone.
I appreciate that this causes some concerns and the new legislation contains several safeguards for developing Orders in Council and regulations in the future. New Orders in Council and proposed regulations will be tabled in this House for consideration. When I referred the subject matter of Bill C-80 to the special committee, I suggested that it may want to consider putting some of the features that I proposed for regulation into the statute itself, but on careful consideration of the use of those two devices the recommendation was to continue
with the proposed plan to use the regulations in addition to the statute in order to provide for specificity, clarity and some flexibility.
If a sufficient number of members of Parliament wish to do so, a resolution to revoke the order or proposed regulation may be put forward. All regulations and Orders in Council under Part III of the Criminal Code will be subject to this procedure. In the near future regulations or Orders in Council for a large number of important gun control matters will be reviewed in this way.
In particular, regulations or orders will be used to prohibit large magazines and designate some military firearms as prohibited or restricted weapons, to set new fees for firearms acquisition certificates and to establish clear, safe storage standards for all firearms owners. These are intended and will be used to create additional certainty and clarity in the interpretation and application of the gun control laws and amendments.
I am strongly committed to developing a stricter and more effective gun control system, but I also recognize that the process must be as open and as accessible as possible. This is an essential part of any democratic society, but it is also good common sense. Some members of this House have suggested that a parliamentary review of regulations will weaken the gun control system. However, the right of review is not open ended, but must be exercised within a particular period of time.
This government is committed to developing tough but workable controls. This requires public scrutiny of the process. Madam Speaker, the fundamental goal of gun control in Canada is to protect the public from firearms violence, while at the same time preserving the interests of legitimate firearms owners and users as much as possible. Regulatory powers are an important tool for this task.
The use of regulations allows the law to focus closely on the firearms, individuals, and situations that raise public safety concerns.
Regulations allow for flexibility in the law to achieve effective gun control in ways that can still permit legitimate activities to continue.
Statutory powers are much broader. Attempting to use them to accomplish regulatory controls on firearms would result in a much less responsive and effective gun control system.
This is why a number of elements of Bill C-17 combine statutory and regulatory components.
The essential elements of the gun control changes I am proposing today are in the legislation, not in the supplementary regulations.
Parental consent, references, and the 28-day waiting period for acquisition certificates are all in the Bill itself. The requirement for a safety course or test is not, because it is already in the Criminal Code. In fact, it has been since 1978.
The prohibitions of converted fully-automatic firearms and large capacity magazines are also in the Bill.
The prohibition or restriction of military or paramilitary firearms is not in the Bill. This is because the power to do this by order in council already exists in the statute itself. No statutory amendment was necessary.

Provisions in the bill will also increase sentences for firearms offences and will increase the use of court prohibitions to include bail and peace bond applications.
I consider all of these things to be key elements of the total package of changes I am proposing today and all of them are included in the bill itself. The other elements, some of which will be the subject of new regulations, are

I have already stated the specific details of the types and capacities of cartridge magazines that will become prohibited weapons by regulation. I have already indicated that the regulations will specify a new FAC fee of $50. They must fit together into a comprehensive and effective package and this will require careful preparation and drafting.
I share the concerns of many members of this House that Canadians expect and deserve improvements of the gun control system as soon as possible. We must also be sure that the job is done properly. Hastily prepared regulations will benefit no one. My commitment is a matter of public record on which I expect to be held accountable. Provisions in a statute may languish for lack of proclamation as have the requirements for training prior to obtaining an FAC. Regulations have the same legal force as statutes and are the essential partners of legislation in a well structured regulatory scheme.
Gun control works. It is probably the oldest and most effective form of crime prevention law, not just here in Canada where it dates back to the last century, but in many other countries as well. It works by ensuring that only those who actually require guns for legitimate purposes can obtain them. Any Canadian who really wants or needs a firearm is free to obtain one provided that he or she can comply with the screening measures. In the United States the use of guns is widely seen as a right. In Canada gun ownership has long been considered a privilege. The history of the Canadian system of gun control dates back not just to 1977-78 but to 1877 when a law was introduced to prohibit the carrying of handguns where there was no reasonable cause to use them for self defence.
As I said a moment ago in French, the west and north were settled peacefully in Canada without the use, by and large, of weapons.
During the debate in the United States on the Brady bill, some very interesting facts were revealed. In the United States, 23,000 people were killed by handguns alone last year. That is 64 people a day. Every day in the United States there are three accidental deaths from handguns alone.
In short, I think Canadians are right to think that our gun control system has made our society less violent. Gun control works and the reasonable extension of gun control without the creation of needless bureaucracy for hunters and trappers is our goal in this debate.
I believe that Canadians want effective gun control. I believe there is a consensus from all sides in this country for effective gun control.
Government Orders
I just want to say something about the chronology of this debate over the last few years, because it helps us to understand where we are at and where we are going.
In 1978 the current gun control law was passed in the House of Commons. I see the member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, who was the minister at the time, is here today. Without going on too much about it, he is one of the members of this House that I very much look up to. He has made an enormous contribution to this House and this country and it is very interesting that he is here today.
He is not a bad hockey player.

My friend says he is not a bad hockey player, too.
That bill is worth looking at. It is the present law. The provisions enforcing mandatory firearms training in that bill, I point out, have not been affected. That is a part of the bill I would still like to see come into force. However, let us look at the bill and the present law.
The 1978 law prohibits automatic weapons. The 1978 law restricts some weapons, including hand guns. The 1978 law makes it mandatory to have a firearms acquisitions certificate and to meet certain criteria to get that certificate, although rather weak criteria I must say. There is a theory stated in the bill that there should be mandatory training before buying a gun. That has not been enacted yet. It really is basically an acquisition system. People who had a gun before 1978 are not involved and people can still get, after 1978, as many guns as they want. Less than 1 per cent of the firearms acquisition certificate applications are turned down. It costs you 10 bucks for a certificate for five years. So, it in itself is a very modest system.
In January, 1989, about a decade later, in Stockton, California a man who said he had a "military hang-up", armed with an AK-47 semi-automatic assault rifle and two pistols, fired 110 rounds from the rifle and killed five children and injured 29 others. This was an indication, it seems to me, of the more and more violent society we have in North America. The state of California responded to the tragedy by banning the sale, possession or manufacture of some semi-automatic weapons. On March 14, 1989, President Bush announced a suspension of the importation of assault weapons. The United States, in some aspects, back in 1989 had a law more advanced than we had with respect to these kind of semi-automatic weapons. That was the impetus for new tougher laws in Canada and was the beginning of the

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
government's commitment, through the previous Minister of Justice, to a tougher gun control law.
In June 1989 the government indicated its intention to introduce fall legislation controlling the importation, possession and sale of semi-automatic and automatic weapons. It received agreement at the federal-provincial ministers' meeting to do that. Then, in December 1989 we had the terrible tragedy at Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal in which 14 young women needlessly lost their lives. In April 1990 a petition was presented to the minister by the students at the Ecole Polytechnique with 516,487 names on it. That total would reach 700,000.
On June 17, 1990, the minister introduced Bill C-80. She announced her firm intention to push the bill through. The intention was not as firm as all that because the bill came to second reading in the House and the bill was diverted to a committee for further study. I will not say any more about that. The fact is that we have the bill back before us.
The committee met and produced a report under the chairmanship of the member for Kitchener. I was proud to be a member of that committee and I would like to acknowledge the work of fellow members on that committee, all of whom did an outstanding job. The member for Rosemont from the Bloc Quebecois also attended the committee and contributed as much as he could to that committee, not being an official member. However, he did show up and contribute and I would like to acknowledge that and the efforts of other members as well.
The committee produced legislation which is now Bill C-17.
Let me deal with Bill C-17 which I have called a modest proposal. Bill C-17 is a somewhat complex proposal. All of us in the debate have received a large number of letters of concern. Many people have really misunderstood the legislation. They think their gun is going to be taken away or they are going to be more affected than they really are. I will give an example.
I had a letter from one of my constituents saying "I am going to be affected". I called the person and found out that he had in fact a non-semi-automatic gun with a bolt action. He was concerned about the magazine size under the regulations in this bill and he felt he would have to
dismantle his gun. It was not true. That was not part of the bill. The magazine size only applies to semi-automatics. It seems to me that we all have a job to do in this House to explain to Canadians just exactly what is in the bill and what is controlled.
First of all, the bill prohibits automatic weapons that have been converted to fire in a semi-automatic mode. These machine guns-and basically they are machine guns-have been brought into Canada in large numbers. The estimate is 15,000 to 50,000 guns in Canada at present. The existing weapons are grandfathered to the present owners. I am glad the minister did not accept the recommendations of the committee. In fact, the department accepted the minority report of the committee not to extend that grandfather. It is bad enough that there is a grandfather provision, but at least it was not extended as the committee wanted to do. There is the first thing: a prohibition of automatic weapons that have been converted to fire in semi-automatic form.
Second, it prohibits a semi-automatic military assault weapon. This is done by regulation and it is not dependent on the bill. As a matter of fact, the minister has the power to do that, I think, under the 1978 law, the old law, and we are still waiting for that.
The problem is this Rambo culture that is growing in the United States where these military assault weapons were produced in surplus by the war machine industries in the United States. Some of them are flowing across the Canadian border. This is what we are aiming at, not at ordinary hunters and trappers in Canada but at this kind of Rambo culture industry that is flooding these weapons into Canada. This is what we should focus on.
There is a real question, however, even after this bill about the Rugez Mini-14. That is a high-powered rapid fire gun. It was used by Marc Lepine, incidentally, in the Montreal massacre. Will it in fact be restricted? Will it be prohibited under this bill?
It will depend on the regulations. We will have to wait. However, the point I am making is that-and I want to repeat it-these are the only firearms whose status is affected by this law. These are the only firearms. It is only the future firearms that are imported. The present ones will be grandfathered and one will be able to sell them to genuine gun collectors. This is a very modest proposal indeed. It is a modest bill. I suggest the minister have a look at the bill. She will see it is a very modest proposal.
June 6, 1991

Third, there is a prohibition on large capacity magazines. That is the other area people are concerned about. There has been more confusion about this proposal than anything else. Again, it is going to be done by regulation with the enabling power of this bill. The limits are as follows: all semi-automatic handguns, a 10-shot limit. This is what the minister has proposed. All centre fire semi-automatic rifles and shotguns, five shots; 22 rim fire rifles, no limit. All bolt, pump or leverage action firearms, no limit.
Therefore, it seems to me that only semi-automatics are affected by this provision. I say to the people who are writing us: "Have a look at actually what is in the bill".
There was a concern expressed by several firearms groups that this proposal would lead to the destruction of thousands of rifles with built-in magazines. However, evidence presented to the special committee shows that of 2,600 makes and models of shotguns and rifles on the market, only 28 are directly affected by the limits. Of these, 26 are military style semi-automatics such as an AK-47. These are precisely the kinds of weapons the limits are supposed to target. Only two weapons, versions of the Marlin Camp carbine, would require modified magazines.
This proposal is an alternative to a ban on all semi-automatics. That is what some groups were advocating. It is a means of limiting fire power.
I remind you, Madam Speaker, that Marc Lepine had a 30-round magazine. The feeling is if that at least could have been limited it might have saved more lives.
There is an exemption here for competition shooters. I have flagged that to have a look at that exemption in committee, again the point being that this is a very modest proposal.
Fourth, in the bill there are changes to the FAC, the firearms acquisition certificate screening process to improve screening: two references, a photograph, a $50 fee, a 28-day cooling off period, and a mandatory training program.
Government Orders
Fifth, safe storage is to be applied to all firearm owners. A genuine gun collector is defined. It seems to me that the genuine gun collector may be a major loophole in the system today. We will have to look at that proposed definition in committee to ensure that it is sufficient. It is a possible area for amendment. I would like also to flag the storage problem. We have got to be flexible on this, deal with it in committee and define it better.
Sixth, there are tougher penalties for firearm usage, although there is not, as the committee recommended, a section 85. That would mean higher minimum sentences for criminals using guns in the course of an offence and, if there is plea bargaining, would ensure that the Attorney General actually does not make it easier for someone who used a gun in a criminal offence. That was not accepted in the bill, although it is in the committee's report.
Finally, there is a parliamentary review of the regulations.
I think it is a modest proposal. The FAC process is strengthened, but no one I think can really call it onerous. There are two types of Rambo weapons which will be prohibited, but only in the future, and the existing weapons will stay. Fire power on semi-automatic weapons will be limited somewhat, so I think it is a modest proposal.
If we were really serious about gun control, really serious, the government would go after all those machine guns, semi-automatic guns and military style weapons, and would really nail them and get them out of this country. There is a lot of wrapping ourselves in good intentions and a little bit of posturing on this. We should really look at this bill again as to how modest it is. We could have gone further.
It was proposed, for example, that there be a registration system and that every gun control supporting group, including the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, the Canadian Police Association, the Caucus of Big City Mayors, the Coalition for Gun Control, the students at Polytechnique, hospital associations and so on. They came before the special committee. The minister's officials said that such a system of actually registering all the guns that are in Canada would not be worth the effort. I find that rather incredible.

June 6, 1991
Government Orders

Personally, I made the following proposal in my report on gun control. Since the restriction on semi-automatic weapons under the present law would effectively prohibit hunting activities, I recommend that all unrestricted, semi-automatic weapons be registered as a separate class of firearms. All future firearms obtained using the FAC, would also be registered at the time of purchase.
Finally, every applicant for a FAC would be required to list all their firearms on the application. This would not place any additional bureaucratic burdens on firearms owners with non semi-automatic rifles who do not need a FAC at present.
This would move us toward a long term goal of a full National Registry System.

There are other weaknesses in the bill, but my time is limited.
I would just like to read a quote from Mr. Lome Newson, the chief provincial firearms officer in British Columbia. I would like to quote from what he told the special committee: "In the first place, these people were very much aware that they were skirting the law by buying superficially modified machine guns. They are deserving of no sympathy." "I am concerned that grandfathering these weapons may overturn the present case law. Presently these guns are declared illegal by law and this bill may actually weaken them."
I want to conclude by saying that we have to look at gun control from differing perspectives. The gun debate is seen as a polarized one. You are either right or wrong, yet it seems to me that there are a number of different points of view. I want to underline three, just briefly.
First of all, I think women have a profoundly different attitude toward guns than men do. Women own only a small percentage of guns in Canada and commit only a tiny percentage of firearms related criminal offences. While women commit less than 5 per cent of firearms homicides, they are the victims of 30 to 40 per cent of such cases.

The massacre at the Ecole Polytechnique focused public attention on the issue of firearms and violence against women. These are issues that have been around for some time.
Sixty per cent of all homicide victims are killed within a family context, and most often, rifles shotguns were used.

I said in my minority report on gun control that no one believes gun control alone is the solution to the problem of violence against women in our society. I think it is part of the solution.
Second, there is a distinct view in rural Canada. One of my members from the Kootenays put it very well. He said: "If a pick-up truck drove up Wellington Street outside the Parliament Buildings and had a shotgun or a rifle in the back, we would freak out. We would be asking, what is going on?" In rural areas of Canada that is quite normal and we must recognize that distinction. We must recognize that people use guns as part of their livelihood. We must recognize that bureaucracy does not work as well in rural areas, so in committee we have to look at safe storage, as well as other provisions.
We helped a little bit in the committee report giving some discretion to rural firearms officers to help rural people, and I think we have to have a further look at that.
I will point out that in rural Canada, a public opinion poll said that three-quarters of the people did support stronger gun control as long as it is effective and fair.
Third, aboriginal concerns. I draw the minister's attention to my minority report. I believe that the federal government is constitutionally bound to consult native people with respect to gun control.
In view of the Sparrow case, the Sioui case and other cases, it may well be that constitutionally and legally this bill and this regime may not apply to native people. This is a debatable question, but there should be concerns not only with the constitutional position of native people but at a minimum, native leadership and native people should be consulted, especially natives living in northern areas.
June 6, 1991

Finally, I have some other concerns which I will flag at committee. For example, I would like to make sure that the film industry in British Columbia is protected and we do not needlessly harm them with needless bureaucracy. That can be raised in the committee because they do use blank, automatic and semi-automatic guns.
I would like to give credit to the Coalition for Gun Control and the work that they have been putting out. That is the group led by Suzanne Edwards, Heidi Rathjen and Wendy Cukier.
I want to say that this debate is changing. If you read the editorials, you will see a lot of support for gun control. You will see them sharing the feeling that I enunciated that the bill is very modest, perhaps too modest. It is not a partisan issue and we have to deal with this.
When you see today: "Gun permits jump by 28 per cent in Toronto," our society unfortunately appears to be becoming more violent.
I want to tell the minister that what we have seen in the course of this debate and in the committee reports is that the people who want gun control, the lobby if you like, for that particular point of view has grown and matured very much. Traditionally there was a view that those who supported gun control were well intentioned but misinformed people. Those who were for less gun control, the gun lobby if you like, would try to bury you with so-called facts.
Now it seems to me that the gun lobby in many ways is sounding emotional and the people who want more gun control are sticking to their facts, are exploring the myths about gun control. Myths like, "guns do not kill people; people kill people". In fact, people without guns injure, people with guns kill. Myths like, "gun control legislation does not reduce gun violence". The fact is that gun control legislation saves lives. The myth that, "what is needed is crime control, not gun control". The fact is that easy access to guns contributes to crime. Look at the studies of Seattle versus Vancouver. Look at the statistics on homicides in Canada.
The myth that people need guns for protection seems to be growing in Canada. The fact is that a home is safer without a gun. These are the debates we are going to hear in the future. This issue is not dead. This issue is just beginning.
Government Orders
Let me conclude by saying that I believe that all Canadians want effective and fair gun control. At the committee stage we are going to make sure this is a workable bill for all segments of the country. We are supporting the bill at second reading. We put the minister on notice that we intend to improve the legislation in committee.

Madam Speaker, this new gun control bill is very disappointing, and I think it shows a clear lack of political courage on the part of the Minister of Justice.
Nearly all legitimate requests from individuals and groups who support gun control were turned down, and most of the proposed measures will be very difficult to enforce. This bill seems more designed to soothe public opinion than to provide effective gun control.
The groups in question estimate that 90 per cent of the bill is about concessions to gun lobbies and only 10 per cent is about improving control measures as demanded by the vast majority of the public.
We were particularly disappointed in the refusal to introduce a firearms ownership licence that would make routine registration of firearms compulsory. We all know that this type of measure is absolutely necessary for genuine gun control.
How many firearms are there in this country? Today, no one can answer that question, and there is nothing in this bill to help provide the answer in the future. Who uses the firearms in this country? Today, no one can answer that question either, and there is nothing in the bill that will provide us with an answer in the future.
The minister expects us to believe the bill will improve gun control. She says quite candidly that she also wants to protect the interests of legitimate firearms users. Would registration unduly restrict their privileges?
The minister knows perfectly well that hunters, for instance, must meet far stricter criteria to exercise their hunting privileges. They have to get an annual licence and conform to very strict wildlife protection regulations.
For instance, in many parts of the country, there is a draw for moose licences. Every year, hundreds of thousands of hunters whose names are not selected are deprived of the privilege of hunting. However, hunters accept this practice because our wildlife must be protected.

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
One wonders why the minister is so timid about protecting public health. Practically all firearms owners I know would be perfectly willing to have firearms licensing and registration, and to pay the requisite fees.
The Minister of Justice knows perfectly well that this type of measure is badly needed. She has implied that the House will probably be asked to pass such a measure in the future. Why not do it now? Just because there is a very small but effective lobby of sellers and owners of firearms who consider that owning a weapon is not a privilege but a right. These people will not tolerate having this privilege subject to a minimum amount of regulation. They are a minority howerever, and this is unacceptable in any civilized society.
Another deplorable aspect of this bill is the procedure selected to exclude weapons we want to prohibit. There is always a risk that regulations are unable to keep up with the latest developments in technology, and they are difficult to enforce, especially for customs officers.
As the hon. member pointed out earlier, why is the weapon used by Marc Lepine at the Polytechnique still not prohibited, eighteen months after this tragic event? How can we tolerate this any longer, especially since this paramilitary weapon is already prohibited elsewhere, even in the United States, for instance in New Jersey?
There is a simple and effective method for changing all this. We must decide that from now on, only legal firearms may be sold in or imported into Canada. Any administrative delay would actually reinforce controls, and when in doubt, customs and the police could refer cases to the appropriate authorities.
Some people will say this will require creating an additional and costly bureaucracy, but why is it easier to import firearms from the United States than to import beer from Belgium? Why are there fewer controls on the purchase and use of firearms in this country than on the purchase and use of sleeping pills? It doesn't make sense.
As for the costs involved, they must of course be kept to a minimum, but not at the expense of public health. In fact, gun control lends itself admirably to the "user pays" principle. Incredibly, the bill fails to prescribe an additional fee for issuing licences and monitoring restricted weapons permits. Why should all taxpayers have to pay for these administration costs? Clearly this is something that will have to be remedied in committee.
Several other aspects of the bill will also have to be thoroughly reviewed. For example, the new regulatory powers regarding safe storage might seem adequate, but how could the minister argue that such regulations will be effective when we won't even know who owns firearms? The fact that there will be storage requirements might make people more careful about the way they store their guns, it would be a kind of education, but it is not, in any way, a real prevention policy.
This bill contains an insidious clause that should be denounced. The whole process of preparing regulations under this act will be done according to an exceptional procedure, which might limit greatly the scope of the act by opening the door to continuing pressure from the gun lobby. As a matter of fact, any proposed regulation or order in Council under this act could be challenged by 20 members or 15 senators who could force a debate and a vote to cancel the said regulation. Such a clause is an open invitation to the gun lobby to pursue its action with a minority of members and senators who oppose gun control.
The minister and the cabinet will hesitate for a long time before introducing regulations or orders in Council which could solidify this opposition to gun control and force a debate in the House. Consequently, this bill imposes self-censorship system on the cabinet which is totally unacceptable and which will lead to a continuing watering down of the required regulations. These clauses must be withdrawn from the bill.
In fact, the bill that is before us and that deals with arms exports and will enable Cabinet to decide to export arms to one country or another, contains no clause enabling members of Parliament to invalidate such provisions. It must be understood that this provision is unique in Canadian laws. I think that the legislative committee will have to ask the minister to backtrack on this issue.
June 6, 1991

Finally, this bill is an unacceptable step back, particularly as regards the prohibition of military or para-military firearms, since it provides for grandfather's rights in the case of present owners. The legislative committee will therefore have to undertake an in depth study in order to transform this rough draft into a real bill providing a legitimate and necessary control of firearms.
In concluding, I would like to mention that the only provision in this bill that deserves unanimous support is the one which provides that, from now on, courts will have to consider issuing prohibition orders regarding the release, on bail or temporary, when the offence was committed by using, attempting to use or threatening to use violence, and when a request is made for an order not to disturb the public peace.
This provision is a real improvement towards real prevention and one that would justify supporting this bill if the other provisions can be improved, notably the withdrawal of the power of revocation in the legislation.
It is still possible for this government to show political will by agreeing on legitimate amendments. I hope that the government will clearly demonstrate this will at the legislative committee. That is why I reserve my judgment until the vote on the committee report.

Mr. Speaker, today marks the 47th anniversary of D-Day: June 6, 1944, the day when the Third Canadian Infantry Division and the Second Canadian Armoured Brigade went ashore on Juno Beach to participate in the invasion which would achieve the liberation of western Europe from Nazi tyranny.
Canadians take pride in knowing that our troops were a major part of this armada. Over 15,000 Canadians, one-fifth of the total allied invasion force, established themselves on the Normandy beaches that day. Our army, navy and air force all played notable roles in the invasion.
Let us bless the memory of those Canadians who fought in this invasion. Let us bless those who did not make it home and were buried in Europe. Let us also bless those who went on to liberate the Netherlands less than a year later. All of them helped to restore freedom.
Mr. Speaker, 47 years ago the prospect of freedom came ashore in Normandy. Let us never forget those who were there for us on that day, and let us never forget those who died for our freedom on D-Day, June 6,1944.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the following statement was made by convicted murderer, Allan George Foster, after sentencing for the murder of three women while on parole. He said: "There is only one thing crazier than me and that is the system that allows me to do what I do".
Many Canadians have become terrified as a result of violent crimes not only by adults but by young offenders. Whether in a mall, a poorly lit street or a parking lot, women are worried about their safety.
One of the root causes of these violent crimes is our justice system, which either renders an all too short prison sentence or grants a too lenient parole.
I call upon the Minister of Justice to address this issue. Let us restore law and order in this country.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the 100th anniversary of the death of Canada's first Prime Minister and first member of Parliament from Kingston, the Rt. Hon. Sir John. A. Macdonald, who is also being recognized at his grave site today in Kingston.
Perhaps, more than any figure in our history, Sir John A. Macdonald is recognized as the driving force behind Confederation. His unwavering conviction that Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia could become prosperous and strong by forming a political union under one flag, serves as a guide for us today as we review our constitutional agreements.
During his political career he was elected to the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Canada seven times and was Prime Minister for 19 years. He is truly the Father of Canada.
On the 100th anniversary of his death, I urge all Canadians to reflect on the trials and obstacles he overcame in order to forge a nation which today is one of the wealthiest in the world.
By capturing the spirit and confidence he held in Canada, we can continue to make our country prosperous and continue to uphold the proud legacy he left behind.

Mr. Speaker, according to a recent public opinion poll, 68 per cent of Canadians outside Quebec and 57 per cent of Canadians in Quebec favour holding a constituent assembly to resolve our national unity crisis.
June 6, 1991

Yet, at the same time, the Minister of Constitutional Affairs was quoted as saying: "The federal government has considered this and now, for several reasons, we have rejected the pure and simple option of a constituent assembly. We have reason to believe it would not be acceptable to Quebec".
Is it any wonder, then, that Canadians feel politicians are not responsive to their wishes and that they have lost faith in the political system and its leadership. If the Prime Minister is really looking for ways to restore the faith of Canadians in this House and in his leadership, he can start by establishing a constituent assembly as favoured by a majority of Canadians, both inside and outside Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, it has been brought to my attention that Revenue Canada is now withholding the goods and services tax credits from persons who qualified for the full GST rebate because they owe back taxes. It is my understanding that Revenue Canada is going back to collect 1986 taxes in order to receive back taxes of lower income Canadians who qualify for the full GST tax rebate. In other words, they are offsetting the GST rebate against back taxes that low income earners owe the government. And when I say low income earners, they are the ones who have the right to the full goods and services tax credit owed.
I don't know how many thousands of low income Canadians have had their rebates taken back to pay back taxes. Usually the rebate would only cover the interest on these back taxes. I think the Minister of National Revenue should spend the weekend and report to the House as to how many people are in involved in the taking away from Canadians of their GST credits.

speechtext:
One hundred years ago today a young Canada mourned the death of a political giant. Sir John A. Macdonald, Canada's first Prime Minister and a Father of Confederation, worked tirelessly to weave the fabric of a young land. From his dream of a national rail link to his battle against the veiled threat of treason of unrestricted reciprocity, Sir John A. shepherded a design for confederation that has held fast for over a century. "Whatever you do, adhere to the union", he stated, "We are a great country and shall become one of the greatest if we preserve it. We shall sink into insignificance if we suffer it to be broken."

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the House seeks to eliminate a subsidy which has outlived its original purpose and has become a burden on the public purse.
The At and East subsidy program was originally introduced in the 1960s to ensure that Canadian grain and flour would move through Canadian ports. The program provided subsidies to the railways based on the difference between the railway's cost and the statutory freight rates dating back to the 1960s. It is worth noting that only a relatively small amount of Canada's export grain moved under this program, less than 3 per cent.
Various studies have been done on this subsidy over the past 15 years. Those subsidies indicated that the subsidy encouraged inefficient movement plus extra handling and storage. It was clear that the program was expensive and no longer necessary. As a result, the subsidy was terminated effective July 15, 1989, as announced in the April 1989 budget.
In order to minimize the impact on users, the legislation provided for a six month transition period to cover grain and flour inventories that were in the rail system on that day.
Members are aware that the government is undertaking a comprehensive review of agricultural policy, which includes an examination of related transportation issues and involves all stakeholders from the farm level through to the consumer.
The principal goal of growing together is to develop options for a national policy which will serve to prepare the Canadian agrifood industry for the challenges of the 1990s and beyond.
Virtually all of the witnesses who appeared before the legislative committee on this bill agreed that the At and East program should be terminated. However, some of the witnesses expressed concern about the impact that terminating the program would have on the two Atlantic grain elevators. In particular, people were worried about the implications that the possible closure of the Halifax grain elevator would have on Atlantic agriculture sectors.
In response to these concerns, the Minister of Agriculture and the minister responsible for grains and oilseeds jointly announced on May 16, 1990, the creation of a steering committee to study the viability of grain handling facilities in the Atlantic provinces.
The steering committee included representatives from industry and the ports, as well as both the federal and provincial governments. The study examined the financial viability of the elevators at Halifax, Nova Scotia, and Saint John, New Brunswick. It also examined the feasibility of a new elevator at Summerside, Prince Edward Island, to handle the increasing volumes of grain being grown in that province.
Proposals put forward by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission and the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Commission, concerning alternatives to
June 6, 1991

the At and East program, were examined as part of the study.
The study concluded that virtually all export grain shipments by rail to both Halifax and Saint John stopped with the termination of the At and East subsidy. The Halifax elevator remained a viable operation because it serviced the Atlantic livestock industry and flour mill in addition to the grain export market.
Unlike the Saint John elevator, it can receive grain by either rail or water. However, the Halifax elevator could be at risk in the longer term unless more export grain can be brought through it.
The study indicated that livestock producers in Atlantic Canada would pay at least $10 more per tonne for feed grains if the Halifax terminal were to close.
The terminal provides an alternative to rail shipping and feed grain to the region as well as competition between rail and water for the feed grain business.
The Saint John elevator, which was almost exclusively handling export grain, closed in May 1990. Unlike the Halifax elevator it was not equipped to receive grain by water.
The study did identify a program that could ensure the long-term viability of the Halifax elevator which is more cost-effective than earlier proposals. This option would be to increase traffic through the Halifax elevator by an additional 200,000 tonnes per year, based on a subsidy of about $3 per tonne.
At the time of the study $3 per tonne was the amount required to equalize the freight rate to Halifax, relative to the St. Lawrence port for grain shipped by water from Thunder Bay. Members will appreciate that it is cheaper to transport bulk products, such as grain, by water than by rail.
One of the main deficiencies of the At and East program was that it subsidized the more expensive rail movements. The government acknowledges the importance of the Halifax grain elevator to the Atlantic livestock and flour milling industries.
I am pleased to advise members that the government is closely monitoring the situation and, if needed, is prepared to ensure that the Halifax elevator remains in operation for the benefit of the Atlantic livestock and flour milling industries.
Government Orders
With respect to the Saint John elevator, the construction of marine unloading facilities and additional storage would be required before the elevator could handle the amount of through-put required to ensure its long-term viability. However, the government is prepared to offer assistance to the Saint John elevator, comparable to what it offered to the Halifax elevator.
In closing, I would like to reiterate that the At and East subsidy is an expensive, inefficient and unnecessary mechanism for supporting grain handling on the east coast. Canadian taxpayers cannot afford a subsidy program based on a 1960 policy which is no longer required.
The government is prepared, however, to minimize the impact of terminating the program on the Atlantic livestock and flour milling industries. Therefore I ask members for their support and approval of Bill C-ll.

Mr. Speaker, under normal circumstances I would be very happy to take part in a debate of this kind. However, as you well know, these are not normal times in our country. Witness the breakdown in the economy. These are not normal times and these are not normal circumstances.
The reason why I am not particularly happy about taking part in this debate is that this bill should not be here in the first place. It does not belong in this House at this particular time. At least, at the very minimum, we should not be debating this bill at third reading. At the very least, this is the day this bill should be introduced. We should not be debating it at third reading.
I say that because this particular bill was introduced a long time ago-more than a year ago-under another name or number and died with prorogation. It died. It died early in the month of May and it should not be in this House. The reason why it is here is that this government broke every tradition in this country, every tradition in this Parliament. It broke every convention that we know of and resurrected this bill along with four others.
