Mr. Speaker, you will recall very well that we went through this kind of debate just a few days ago. Never before in the history of our Parliament have we ever resurrected a bill without unanimous consent. It has never happened in the Mother of our Parliaments in England, in Great Britain.
In my opinion we are debating this bill today as a result of contempt for our traditions, contempt for this House, and ultimately I believe contempt for the Canadian people. Nevertheless, we have it here. I just want to remind you that this bill, in its previous incarnation, was brought out of committee on May 31, 1989. That is more than a year ago. It was debated at report stage and concurred in on June 5, 1990. That is a year and one day ago.
This government had all the time in the world to finish this bill. It had ample time, but it mismanaged and bungled as usual. Here we are, the government breaking tradition, breaking convention and resurrecting a bill that really died at prorogation in early May.
It is little wonder that this kind of debate at this particular time is kind of vexing. It leaves me a little angry, but we have it. I guess we are going to have to live with it and we are going to debate it.
We might recall-I will just provide a little more history-that the bill, which was designed to eliminate the At and East subsidies, was actually brought in after the subsidies were already eliminated.
The subsidies were eliminated back in July 1989. Some time after that the bill was brought in to confirm something that the government had already done.
In my opinion, that is just more contempt for the traditions of this House.
It was said at the time the bill was brought in, more than a year ago, that it would have harmful effects across the board, particularly in the maritimes.
I am sad to say that some of those forecasts have already come true. I would think that most of the other forecasts will be confirmed in the months to come or at least in the years to come.
Let us look at the facts. They are indisputable. First of all, the elevator at Saint John is gone. It is closed. It is no more. There were 55 jobs lost. In a region of Canada like
Atlantic Canada that is particularly painful. Losing 55 jobs is nothing to be sneezed at.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport said a few minutes ago in his remarks that this legislation, the At and East legislation, had outlived its usefulness and had become a burden on the public treasury.
Of course, we all know that this government does everything in the name of deficit reduction.
It has outlived its usefulness. I wish that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport would say that to the 55 people in Saint John who lost their jobs. I wonder whether they would agree. I doubt it very much.
Not only that, it has already had an impact on the elevator at Halifax, Nova Scotia. There are serious ramifications for that facility. Already, according to figures that I secured just today, 27 jobs have been lost at the Halifax elevator.
That is a loss of $14.4 million to the Halifax economy. If that elevator, which is in a precarious situation, closes it will mean an additional $13.2 million lost to the economy in Halifax. When it comes to jobs it will mean an additional loss of 220 person-years.
We are talking about a very serious situation.
The Halifax elevator, according to information that was given to me today, needs about 260,000 tonnes to break even. It is just at that figure now. It is operating at around that figure, so if it drops below that the Halifax facility is in trouble and it could close.
That is very disturbing. It is a very important facility to the city of Halifax.
Mr. Speaker, I want to remind you of something that my colleague from Halifax said in this House back on February 12, 1990. She was taking part in the debate on the legislation at the time and she said: "Halifax is a city that depends on its ports. The grain elevators, the activity produced by the grain elevators and the jobs created thereto are part of the relative economic health of the city of Halifax."
I say relative because it is relative to the ill health of the rest of the region. That ill health in the rest of the region has been caused by the poison dart of government policy.
June 6, 1991

Then ray hon. friend from Halifax continued, and I quote again:
There is no particular reason, other than a government devoted to a Canada that does not exist outside the very central part of our geography, to see our regions die, and yet they are dying. They are dying from a lack of interest. They are dying from an interest that can only be described as poisonous and that can only be described as anti the best interests of large numbers of Canadian citizens.
That is what my colleague from Halifax said in this House on February 12, 1990. When we are talking about the Halifax elevator, we are talking about something that is crucial to the economy of that city.
As a result of the At and East subsidy elimination, there has been an increase in the cost of transportation to the tune of about $10 a metric ton. This is in line with predictions and forecasts that were made by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission some time ago. Unfortunately the assessment-I say unfortunately because the assessment by the APTC was somewhat alarming-their forecasts are coming true.
While I am talking about the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, this is what it said about the termination of the At and East program. It said that when it comes to grain elevators, the impact-that is, a loss to the economy- would be $3,735,000; the flour mill in Halifax, another $3,200,000; additional cost of livestock and poultry feed, another $8 million; local grain production, $950,000; port and railway employment, $8,280,000. The total identifiable impact on the Atlantic provinces through the termination of the At and East program came to just over $34 million.
Also the Canadian Transport Commission some time ago in its assessment of the At and East program pointed out that the program was responsible in the way of transportation for about 330 jobs; milling in western Canada, another 295 jobs; 75 more jobs at Georgian Bay port; 85 more jobs at Halifax and St. John's; and 402 jobs when it comes to milling in central Canada.
Another thing that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission pointed out is that if the At and East legislation proceeded to the bitter end, and it looks like it is going to happen-of course the subsidies are all gone-the buyers in the provinces who normally relied on grain from western Canada would have to turn
Government Orders
elsewhere. They would have to turn to countries like the United States and to countries in western Europe.
I do not think that makes the people in Atlantic Canada very happy. In fact, I was listening to a speaker from Atlantic Canada in one of our earlier debate. He in effect said that Atlantic Canadians are good Canadians. They want to belong to Canada. They want to participate fully in the Canadian economy. It pains them, it grieves them a lot, if they are forced to turn to other countries for their supplies.
I think it is a dam shame that the Atlantic provinces will have to look elsewhere for their feed grain. In fact, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Committee has already suggested that there be an elimination of the countervail on U.S. com. It is a ridiculous situation. Here we have a countervail to protect our producers in this country, and now we have in effect Canadians pitted against Canadians. This is the situation we face. Atlantic Canadians who normally buy their feed grain from other Canadians, especially in western Canada, will perhaps have to turn to the United States or to western Europe. Does that make sense? I do not think it does. Of course it is a blow to the west, particularly at this time. I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it is tough times down on the farm these days. Farmers will be very happy to grab on to any market, small or big, to maintain their survival. Western farmers do not want to lose one dollar of market in Atlantic Canada. This is what the elimination of the At and East subsidies has done.
I think that perhaps one of the problems we have here is that this government never really understood the purpose of the At and East legislation. Earlier we heard the parliamentary secretary talk about the legislation outliving its purpose. Well, what was its purpose?
Let me go back exactly 25 years to 1966 when the legislation was brought in. At that time the new legislation or the proposed legislation was spoken to by a very venerable, honourable occupant of this House, a man no less than J. W. Pickersgill. You probably know him. What did Mr. Pickersgill say at the time? Describing the purpose of the At and East legislation Mr. Pickersgill said: "To ensure that we will have rates which will provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of the Atlantic ports".

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
In other words what Mr. Pickersgill was saying at the time, in addition to ensuring that eastern Canadian ports could compete with U.S. ports, was that the At and East rates were also intended to enable the ports of Halifax and Saint John to compete with Montreal and other St. Lawrence River ports. That was the original purpose of the At and East legislation.
The other thing I would like to point out is that the At and East legislation really was in keeping with the history of this country. What we have done over 124 years is defy the physical make-up of this country, defy our geography. What we did was build up parallel systems to what was available in the United States because under normal conditions and forces the pull north-south. If the nation-builders in the early days of this country had ignored the realities of Canada and the north-south forces, this country might not have lasted. It certainly would not have lasted 124 years. But it lasted and prospered because we had statesmen, politicians, and nation-builders with vision and a strong belief in this country. They established programs and legislation to ensure the future of this country. The building of the CPR is an example, as is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the creation of the Canadian Wheat Board and the At and East program. I could go on and on.
The At and East program is in keeping with our heritage. It is in keeping with our history. It really carries the spirit of Canada, yet this government is saying to heck with all that. It does not care about that. It is not interested in that. It is interested in something else.
No wonder this country is in a state of confusion. No wonder this country is going down hill. No wonder Canadians feel alienated. No wonder Canadians are obsessed with their cynicism. They have a government and particularly a Prime Minister who does not understand the history of this country, who does not understand what this country is all about. At and East is part of that.
At and East was just part and parcel of an orderly marketing system which we had built up over many long years. These things did not happen just overnight. These
things did not happen over a weekend or two. It took years and years to build.
Over the years we have built up an orderly marketing system. In that orderly marketing system we have now all kinds of marketing boards. Also within that orderly marketing system we have a supply management system.
Despite some of the grievous problems that we have, particularly when it comes to grain farming in this country, those institutions that we have developed over the last number of decades have served Canadians well, are serving Canadians well and I would submit will continue to serve Canadians well provided that this government stops its dam tinkering and tampering.
There is concern that under this government the unravelling of our programs will continue. It is not just a matter of At and East, it goes well beyond that.
In this House about a year ago or so we witnessed the government putting the kibosh on the interest-free advance payments for crops. There was a great outcry because of that. Prairie producers in particular said: "No, it was wrong. It was an effective program. It was not a costly program. It paid all Canadians in the long run". Fortunately, after a great outcry, after a lot of pressure on the government, the government did change its mind. For how long? We can never be sure. When it comes to this government we have to be ever vigilant.
There is more. It is not only At and East and the interest-free advance payments for crops, there are other programs and institutions at risk. Take for example the Canadian Wheat Board, the venerable Canadian Wheat Board which has served Canadians well. In particular, it has served grain farmers well in this country.
The wheat board is in great danger, I submit. We know that it is now in a serious deficit situation. It is perhaps looking at a deficit of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $700 million, $800 million, $900 million, perhaps as much as $1 billion. I am not suggesting when I cite those figures that the government is totally responsible for that deficit. There is a terrible international subsidy war going on and it is costing the wheat board a lot of money. Where does the wheat board get its money? From Canadian taxpayers.
June 6, 1991

I do submit that the government has put the Canadian Wheat Board at risk. How? One way is by allowing American wheat into this country.
Under the free trade agreement if the subsidy level in Canada reached that of American subsidies, there was a clause triggered in the FTA that meant Americans would have the right to come in and sell their wheat in Canada.
Unfortunately, the subsidy levels in the two countries met some months ago and it was decided just a few weeks ago that American wheat had to come in.
That poses a terrible risk to the Canadian Wheat Board.
Right off the bat, it cost the Canadian taxpayers $25 million. For the Canadian Wheat Board to compete with the lower priced subsidized American wheat, it would have to drop its prices, and it did. It will cost the Canadian taxpayers $25 million.
There is more to it than that. Once you allow American wheat to come in, you trigger another set of dynamics. I think I have said it before in this House and I will say it again.
When farmers, especially those who live near the U.S. border, see American wheat coming into this country, they are going to look at the American market and say to themselves: "If American wheat can come into our country, maybe we can sell our wheat directly into the American market. We will not have to go through the Canadian Wheat Board. We will find a little niche market here and there, and we will sell our wheat at perhaps a higher price than that offered by the Canadian Wheat Board."
If that happens, and it surely will, one can appreciate the kind of pressure that is going to put on the Canadian Wheat Board.
You cannot have the Canadian Wheat Board, in effect, selling wheat for some Canadian farmers and not for others. You cannot have it that way.
It has to have exclusive jurisdiction or it is going to be out of action completely. I am really afraid for the future of the Canadian Wheat Board.
We hear all kinds of comments from the Conservatives on the other side, this government, saying: "Our faith in the Canadian Wheat Board is solid. Do not worry. We are right behind the Canadian Wheat Board 100 per cent, so all your talk about possible doom and gloom when it comes to the Canadian Wheat Board is totally and completely off the mark."
Government Orders
I do not think I am wrong, and I also know that this is a right wing government. It really does not believe that the government has a place in the economy. It really believes in laissez faire, and so when it talks about supporting the Canadian Wheat Board I really wonder.
The other thing when we are talking about American wheat coming into this country is what the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said: "Hold it. We do not want American wheat coming into Canada at this particular time because we have some unfinished business."
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture took the position that its members were not afraid of competition. They were not afraid of taking on the Americans. Their product is just as good as that of the Americans. They are just as efficient as the Americans and so they were not afraid of competing with the Americans. However, as I said, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture took the position that there was some unfinished business. As long as Americans were raiding our traditional export markets, as long as the Americans were using their so-called Export Enhancement Program to raid our markets, it was the position of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to say and say bluntly to the Canadian government: "Don't let American wheat come into this country until that other serious matter is resolved".
In my opinion the position taken by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and others made a lot of sense. The Americans play hardball; they are tough negotiators. You don't mess around with the Americans. If you are going to deal with the Americans, you take them on and you take them on frontally, directly. You don't mess round. You don't play games. You take them on directly. I think that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had the right idea. If the Americans want access to our market when it comes to their wheat, then they had better lay off our traditional markets elsewhere around the world.
Now you ask why they should lay off our traditional markets elsewhere around the world. After all, is competition not just competition? It may sound that way, but under the free trade agreement, the infamous free trade agreement, there was an agreement with respect to this matter of one country raiding the traditional markets of the other. I refer to Article 701.4 of the free trade agreement. In that article it says: "The U.S. and Canada

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
are to take into account the effects of their export subsidies on other nations to avoid prejudicing each other's markets".
That is a direct quote. That is what Article 701.4 of the FTA says. There is another article as well and that article is 2011. What does it say? That article stipulates that if one party causes nullification or impairment of any benefit reasonably expected to access to that party directly or indirectly under the provisions of this agreement, that party may, with a view to the satisfactory resolution of the matter, invoke the consultation provisions of the Article 1804 and, if it considers it appropriate, proceed to dispute settlement pursuant to Articles 1805-1807 or, with consent of the other party, proceed pursuant to Article 1806.
There you have it, Mr. Speaker. Under the free trade agreement we had a right to take the Americans on, to resolve this matter with respect to their raiding of our traditional markets. As I said, I think the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and others had it right when they said: "Until that Export Enhancement Program problem is resolved, don't let any American wheat come into our country".
Do you know what members of the government said or did? Absolutely nothing. They did nothing. They would not go to bat for our producers. They would not go to bat for our consumers. They would not go to bat for the country. They had all the right. Not only did they have the legal right under the FTA, I submit to you that they had the moral right on behalf of all Canadians to get some kind of justice out of the situation. However they said no, and I think that is abominable.
I think it is terrible that our government would not go to bat on behalf of our farmers. Then again, I guess it really should not come as any great surprise. As I said earlier, this is a laissez-faire government. It believes in the unfettered market driven economy.
Hear, hear.

Yes, there is my hon. friend from Calgary confirming it. According to these anti-diluvian thinkers, according to these dinosaurs, we should close down our democracy, close down our governments. "There is no place for government in the economy. We
will just leave it to the boys out there in the marketplace. We will just leave it to the boys and they will do us justice and they will do well. We will have the old trickle down theory and all that nonsense".
You know dam well that is pure, utter hogwash, pure, utter nonsense.
It is not an accident that just days ago the United Nations declared Canada, according to its human development index, the second best country in the world. The United States is number seven, by the way.
Do you think it is really just an accident that relative to other countries in the world Canada is a veritable paradise? Was that just an accident? Not on your life.
We are a great country. This a country that is one of the greatest in the world because we had visionary leaders in this country. Through our democracy they wisely and very judiciously used the instrument of government for the betterment of human development to build our economy and raise our standard of living.
I do not ask government to be oppressive. I do not ask government to take over and run everything. I do not ask government to own everything. There is a place for government. After all, if we are a democracy-and this is a democracy-we must have an instrument to express our democratic will. We do that through the instrument of government, yet we have this anti-diluvian government that is more like a 19th century or 17th century government that says: "to heck with all that tradition, to heck with our history, and to heck with all our economic successes of the past number of decades, we have a better way. We have a laissez-faire way. We have a right wing agenda to pursue and, you know what, they don't listen to us".
I think that we have seen in the past little while that government policies are not working. Just look at the economic indices. Look at the economic numbers. The Tory approach is the wrong way. They are taking us down the hill. I want to say that I think it unfortunate, as I conclude my remarks, that we are debating this bill at this particular time.
As I said at the top, it should not be here at all. I wish the government would rethink, but I know that is hoping
June 6, 1991

in vain. The subsidy is all wrong. That is their opinion. I guess we are wasting our time, but I think it is important we put these thoughts and these comments on the record. I have done that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is again hardly a delight to participate in the debate today on Bill C-ll, an act to amend the Railway Act regarding grain and flour subsidies. I do want to say from the start that the purpose of this bill, interestingly enough, is to eliminate the At and East grain transportation subsidy given to shippers of export grain and flour from Thunder Bay through the ports of Saint John and Halifax in Atlantic Canada.
What is interesting about this legislation that the government has brought forward is really two points in terms of process. One is that this is all after the fact. This particular support for the grain industry, to encourage the viability of the elevator at Halifax and the elevator at Saint John, as well as the viability of the livestock industry throughout Atlantic Canada and to provide an essential role in the delivery of competitive priced feed grains to the maritimes, to say nothing of the flour mills and the thousands of thousands of people both directly and indirectly employed by the movement of grain into the Atlantic region, was done away with months ago. As a matter of fact, it was months and months ago. Now we are debating legislation to legitimize what the government did in the past. This is retroactive legislation.
This is not the way to run a government. No wonder the people of Canada are cynical, disappointed and disillusioned. It is no wonder that so many Conservative friends of mine in western Canada shudder when the name of the Prime Minister is mentioned. They are now joining the Reform Party in leaps and bounds as a legitimate, I suppose, conservative party in western Canada and elsewhere, as we are seeing in the papers.
They feel if you have a government and you want to pursue a particular course of action, the usual process is to introduce legislation, take it through the various stages: first reading, second reading, committee stage, report stage, third reading, and then through the other House.
Government Orders
This government has that sort of "father knows best" approach. It has this big brother approach to government that says: "We know what is best for this industry, this region, this community or this sector of the economy, and we are going to just do this with the stroke of a pen or a hack of an axe. Later, if we have the opportunity or some time in the future, we will legitimize what we have done". That is how dictatorships work. That is how totalitarian regimes operate. That is not how a democracy operates, where the duly elected people of Canada participate in a decision: a vote is taken and, if the majority supports an initiative, then that is that.
It is a bit biased, because in this case we have a large Conservative majority and it tends to carry the day. Nevertheless, normally one would expect Parliament to go through those various stages.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: You are a little biased in your remarks, Nelson.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend says I am biased in my remarks. Indeed, as my good colleague indicates, I am. I cannot believe we are actually doing this. I feel dirtied by participating in this process, which I really deem to be bordering on totalitarianism. The government just says: "Forget about Parliament. Forget about democracy. Forget about the opposition voices. Forget about the legislative committees we have in the House of Commons. Forget about the backbenchers of the Conservative Party. The cabinet just made a decision and that is it, and you had bloody well better accept it. If you do not, it does not matter anyway because we have abandoned all this support for the Atlantic grain industry".
That troubles me. It troubles me as a parliamentarian. It troubles me a democrat. It troubles me as a New Democrat, that somehow we are once again seeing the government ignore and abuse the House of Commons. However that has now become a theme. I guess we just have to simply be part of this process and do the best we can.
That is why we have opposed this legislation. Not only do we think it is bad legislation for Canada and a terrible legislation for the Atlantic region, but it is an inappropriate way to proceed.
I know my hon. friend across the way, who is sitting in listening to these debates, shares my concerns. I know he must share the feelings I have, but unfortunately he is

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
not in a position to really do much. However I sense in his heart of hearts that he has agreed with my comments and particularly those of the previous speaker who had a very thorough deliberation on this issue.
That is one concern. Another concern is that this bill used to be called not Bill C-ll but Bill C-26. Bill C-26 was a bill from the previous session. I emphasize the previous session because at the end of the previous session all of the bills the government was dealing with normally just die on the Order Paper. That is the end. It is a new beginning. It is the end of that session and the beginning of a new session. The government introduces a throne speech, the Governor General sits in the Senate and reads out the new agenda for the government and it starts anew.
That is what usually takes place and it is what most governments have done. As a matter of fact, it is what all governments have done in Canadian history. It is what has happened in the United Kingdom year after year, decade after decade for hundreds of years.
However, this government said: "We have a new idea. We are going to ignore what happens at prorogation". Bill C-26 ought to have died on the Order Paper, as has been done now for hundreds of years in the parliamentary tradition. The government decided to bring in a Draconian piece of legislation, a motion that reinstated this bill and simply said: "Let us now call it C-ll and we will pick up where we left off".
That is not right. It is not the parliamentary thing to do. It is not the democratic thing to do. It is not something that would be done in any serious Parliament of the world, and yet that is what we have had done here.
It is very discouraging to have to participate in this process which I consider to be inappropriate democratically. Also, the fact that we are debating legislation to legitimize a decision the cabinet took months and months ago seems obviously not to be the kind of practice found in a democratic society and during the continuation of a democratic process.
However, having said that, let me just indicate why some of us have been so intent on stopping this legislation. This legislation would have done a great deal for Atlantic Canada. I do not think there is anybody in Canada who would disagree that any support, encouragement and development that we can encourage and initiate in Atlantic Canada is good, not just for the people living in Atlantic Canada, but good for the country. If it is good for the country it is good for all regions of Canada.
As a result of the At and East Program, as it has been referred to, a few years ago the grain elevators in Saint John and Halifax had an economic impact of $3,735,600 a year. That is substantial. The flour mill in Halifax alone had an economic positive impact of $3,200,000 each year. For the hundreds and hundreds of families involved in the livestock industry in Atlantic Canada the cost saving to allow them to participate, not only in livestock but in the poultry business as well, amounted to an annual amount of $18,160,000. That was a tremendous level of support the federal government was providing for the livestock producers and people using grain, as I say, poultry growers as well.
Local grain production benefited by $950,000 a year. The port and railway employment benefited by $8,280,700 a year. Those were the men and women involved with the elevators, the port facilities and the railway systems in that area, a substantial number of people, hundreds and hundreds of them.
The total identifiable impact on the Atlantic provinces amounted to $34 million-plus each year.
I read the other day with interest an account in one of the financial papers commenting on the situation in Atlantic Canada regarding this legislation. It said that the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Commission indicated that the economics of grain traffic at the port in 1988 amounted to $25.9 million in revenues and 263 jobs, while flour traffic resulted in $28.4 million in revenues and 220 jobs.
A substantial number of people are employed, then, in the elevator industry as well as the flour industry. In Saint John, the Saint John Port Commission put out an information program which indicated that the movement of bulk grains through its port back in 1988 under At and East program amounted to $8.5 million and was responsible for 90 direct jobs.
That in itself is very impressive. In other words, because of the At and East program, hundreds and hundreds of Atlantic Canadian men and women were meaningfully employed. Those were direct jobs. As we know, for everyone directly employed at the elevator, at the flour mill, at the port, on the railway or in other related activities like livestock producers and so on, there are other people that depend on them. I am talking now about the dentists, the school teachers, the bus drivers, people working in retail stores and so on and so forth. In other words, we can talk about the hundreds of
June 6, 1991

direct jobs, but also let us be cognizant of the fact that there are hundreds and hundreds of indirect jobs that are related to these permanent positions.
The government, in its wisdom, has decided to eliminate the grain support from central and western Canada. The Halifax elevator plays a vital role as a grain storage facility. Without it Cover Flour Mill, the only flour mill in Atlantic Canada, would likely be forced to close.
The Halifax elevator requires 260,000 tonnes a year to make it a viable facility. At the moment it is perilously close to moving below that. If that occurs in any substantive way the elevator would be forced to close down its operations partly or wholly and move hundreds of people out of full-time meaningful employment.
Without the Halifax elevator shipping feed grains by light vessel through the Port of Halifax, the only competitive alternative to rail transport, would no longer be possible. Based on past experience, this would result in an increase in the rail rates for domestic feed grains of at least $10 a tonne.
The livestock industry in the maritimes depends on grain from Ontario and western Canada. If the transport costs go up by $10 a tonne it is estimated that 5,000 jobs will be lost in the livestock industry, the feed mills, meat packing plants and dairies. I think that bears repeating. If the transportation costs go up by $10 a tonne it is estimated that 5,000 jobs will be lost.
For some people in the House of Commons losing
5.000	jobs may not be considered a major issue. Large plants in central Canada can close down and 2,000 or
3.000	people lose their jobs. Unfortunately, under the free trade agreement that has become a reality, a regular news item now in many of the regional newspapers. This is sad, it is disappointing, it is regretful, but under the free trade agreement this has become a reality.
In Atlantic Canada losing five jobs is serious. Fifty jobs is a major issue. Five hundred jobs is a regional crisis, and 5,000 jobs is an absolute, total disaster. Yet, that is what the impact of this legislation will do to Atlantic Canada.
Government Orders
I do not understand why people, particularly on the government side from Atlantic Canada, are not standing up and ranting and raving about the absolute lunacy of proceeding with this legislation, are not lobbying the cabinet and lobbying their colleagues to stop this sort of pell-mell run into a major economic crisis. Yet, there seems to be no sound whatsoever coming from the government benches.
If the Halifax grain elevator is required to close because the 260,000 tonnes a year are not realized, that will result in the loss of 283 jobs in the port itself. Another 250 indirect jobs may be lost as well, as I said earlier. Closure of the Dover Flour Mills would result in another 45 jobs being lost and the loss of a local market for producers of milling wheat.
In Ontario four grain elevators have been shut down because At and East has been cancelled-two in Midland, one in Port McNicoll and one in Prescott.
The Ontario flour mills have lost export contracts and require lower wheat prices to compete with Quebec mills for CIDA contracts. At the same time, Ontario farmers are already receiving record low prices and cannot afford to see their prices drop any further.
One can go on and on. I do not think that is necessary. We have to ask: "Who gains by this? Who benefits from this legislation?"
Previous speakers and I have pointed out that hundreds and hundreds of people who live in Atlantic Canada will be losers. A major livestock sector will be a loser. The poultry sector will be a loser. The flour milling will be a loser. Local grain producers will be in difficulty. The people who work in ports and elevators will be losers.
Who gains? Surely, the government must be helping somebody with this particular initiative. Interestingly enough, the winners of the loss of the At and East program are places in central Canada, primarily Montreal, but also ports in Ontario since Halifax and Saint John cannot compete with the St. Lawrence rates.
There is a deep unfairness in that the St. Lawrence seaway is subsidized several millions of dollars annually by the federal government through the provision of free ice-breaking, dredging and other Transport Canada services. While the support for the Great Lakes and the

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
St. Lawrence seaway operations continue, the support for the Atlantic system is removed, which essentially is cutting off the lifeline for all those people in Atlantic Canada.
I simply want to summarize my remarks by suggesting that this is part of the way the Conservative government has been progressing.
In other words, let the free market decide what happens in Canada. Imagine if previous governments had done that. If they had simply allowed the American and the Yankee to and fro economic forces to dominate right across Canada, we would not have a country. There would be no Canada.
We were celebrating today the 100th anniversary of John A. Macdonald's death. One hundred years. Here was a leader of the Conservative Party with a vision of Canada: rails across the country and appropriate programs to support Canadian industry and create jobs from coast to coast to coast. He had a vision and a commitment to Canada as a country; something separate, an identity separate from the United States. It would be a way of life, a country and a vision of the future that was separated completely from that of the United States.
Today, we have exactly the opposite. We have a government with no vision at all, quite prepared to sell Canada to the United States in whatever form, and the sooner the better. Here is a government that is removing all sorts of programs which link up Canada and Canadians.
Today we are debating one. It is an opportunity for Canadians in the House of Commons to stand up and say: "Enough is enough". The At and East legislation will eliminate one of the critical and crucial lifeblood systems in the economics of Atlantic Canada forever.
We do not have to allow this to happen. We do not have to see this occur. That is why I am begging my colleagues opposite to do the right thing: stand up and support Atlantic Canada.
If we do not, all of the action is going to continue to flow economically into central Canada. As a result of the free trade agreement with the United States-God forbid if we ever get into the free trade agreement with Mexico as well-if we continue erosion of the economic
activity southward into the sun belt and into northern Mexico, that is where the economic action will be in North America.
That is where the jobs will be. That is where the synergy of economics and financial investment will occur. It will not be in Atlantic Canada. It will not be in Canada, period.
This is an opportunity for us within our own area of jurisdiction to stand up and say: "Let's do something for Atlantic Canada that is meaningful."

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address remarks to Bill C-ll amending the Railway Act. I say to the member from British Columbia of the New Democratic Party, first and foremost, the At and East is dead. It has been dead since July 16, 1989. There is absolutely no point voting against the bill because nothing in the world will resurrect the At and East.
The grain products that were moving under the At and East subsidies ceased to move prior to July 16, 1989, and all we are dealing with is a legal technicality, one that should have been put to rest in the last session of Parliament. Why should it have been put to rest? Apparently the member from British Columbia of the New Democratic Party does not know. It should have been put to rest so we can get on with remedying the situation and to establish set-offs to the cancellation of the At and East that will benefit the port of Halifax and hopefully other east coast ports.
It is very disturbing to hear members of Parliament from other regions of Canada, no matter how well meaning or how good their intentions, to wax so eloquently on an issue that now has been put to rest in the area affected; Nova Scotia and the east coast ports. Let me explain why. There has not been one gallon, not one tonne of grain or grain products moving through the port of Halifax or any other east coast port under the At and
June 6, 1991

East for approximately two years. Everybody should be clear on that.
Let us look at the positive side to which we have been trying to move for that same two year period, the assets to At and East. Even organizations like the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission representing the governments of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have said: "Eliminate the At and East."
The At and East was involved in expenditure over the years of approximately $40 million by the Government of Canada. What the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission wanted was all or a portion of that money to be spent on other transportation initiatives affecting not only marine transportation but the agriculture industry.
What were some of those offsets? We have had this in the House of Commons before. They are all on record. They have been before standing committees on transport and in various other places. Let me briefly list some of the offsetting items that were talked about by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, by the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Commission and by many other organizations.
One of the things that would offset the cancellation of the At and East and reduce the negative and adverse aspects of the cancellation would be utilization of unit trains to move grain to Halifax. We have for other reasons the possibility of the double-stacking of railway containers which would perhaps be a part of those kinds of railway line improvements.
This has been done in western Canada. Under the grain transportation system additional cars were provided by other agencies such as the government of Alberta, and so more people and agencies can provide better facilities for land transportation of grain. We can make better use of water transportation systems to Atlantic ports for feed grains. We can eliminate countervails on some of the U.S. products such as com and use those products in Atlantic Canada. We could help the port of Saint John by improving the facilities there for the handling of grain products, and we could promote the export of flour from the port of Halifax with suitable attractions. We could also provide for export permits for feed grains to and from other foreign countries including
Government Orders
the United States. We have all of these possible offsets listed, but we are not able to get on with the business of reducing and mitigating the impact of the cancellation of the At and East because it has been held up in Parliament. It has been in limbo for two years. That limbo was created by the opposition, and not always opposition members from Atlantic Canada who knew what was at stake but opposition members like the member of the New Democratic Party from British Columbia.
Let me digress to say that this very weekend the New Democratic Party is having a convention in Halifax. I hope while the New Democratic Party members are in Halifax they will seek the opportunity to consult with port officials and others actually involved, not armchair socialists but people actually involved in marine transportation and in the shipment of grain and grain products. I hope they will say to them: "What do you want us to do in Parliament? Do you want us to continue to hold up the finalization of the cancellation of the At and East, or do you want us to pass the legislation and get on with mitigating the disadvantages of the cancellation of the At and East?"
I am sure they will hear from everyone-port officials, stevedores-to get on with the business of mitigating the adverse impact of the cancellation of At and East.
I stand in the House once more to appeal to the opposition to get this legislation passed. The At and East is gone. There are no grain products moving in Canada on the basis of subsidization through the At and East provision. It is over. As I said at the outset, it is a dead issue; do not prolong it.
Let me talk about the port of Halifax and marine transportation in general. Again, we have those awful armchair socialists in the New Democratic Party reading briefing notes supplied by God knows who and getting up in the House of Commons making speeches about subjects of which they have little or no knowledge.
I am not trying to make remarks in their absence. I know they are all heading to Halifax, and I hope they spend their money there, but unfortunately there are no members of the New Democratic Party present in the House. However, in case they read the record, and I am not saying that any of them take the trouble to read any

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
good material, let them note this. The marine transportation industry is international. It goes across the world.
If you are building a $50 million to a $100 million vessel and you are providing a crew and all the equipment necessary, you take that vessel anywhere you want to go in the world. Anyone in the marine transportation business knows that they have to compete world-wide. It has nothing to do with arrangements with the United States of America. It has nothing to do with loyalty to the North Atlantic routes. They are captive of no one in the marine transportation industry. They go where they get the best deal. They go where they get the best facility.
If Canadian ports do not provide the best facilities and the best arrangements, the marine transportation community operating massive fourth generation container ships and other vessels will go elsewhere. We have got to compete.
There is no way to protect Canada or Canadians in the marine transportation industry. Get it through your heads in the New Democratic Party and in the Liberal Party that this is not Canadianism at stake. We cannot have a made-in-Canada marine transportation policy. We might have a made-in-Canada shipbuilding policy- and we can debate that at another time-but we cannot have a made-in-Canada marine transportation policy.
Do not talk about the United States of America. Do not talk about arrangements with Europe. We have to compete with everyone, and they are from Hong Kong. They are from Taiwan. They are from Korea. They have massive ships. They have the crews to operate them, and they do not have to go to any ports. There is always a port they can find that will accommodate them. The issue is competition. You have to be competitive. The very word these armchair socialists don't like. They hate that word "competition". What happens is they come into the House of Commons and they tell members and the public that we do not need to compete, and that is simply not true. It might be true when you are growing grain and subsidizing it. I don't know about that. It may be true in some areas. But, for heaven's sake, understand it is not true in marine transportation. It is not true in the port business. This is why I want everybody to
know, and if I have to say it louder I will: "We have to compete".
They understand that in the port of Halifax. The Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Commission, the Halifax Port Commission, everybody connected with marine transportation understands it. It is the first thing they will tell you: you have to compete. You have to compete with New York. You have to compete with Montreal. You have to compete with Baltimore. In order to get the business you have to provide the facilities.
Now, let me talk about the port of Halifax, if I finally got that point through to anybody who is interested in that subject. My questions are about the port of Halifax, as an example. Somebody else can make a speech for the port of Saint John. Maybe my good friend from Carleton County will make that speech. For the moment I am going to talk about the port of Halifax, because there are real difficulties in the port of Halifax. They are caused by the pressure of international competition. How are we going to react to these pressures that make the port of Halifax not competitive in some areas?
First of all, we have to have a level field among Canadian ports. That is to say, neither the port of Halifax nor the port of Montreal, nor any other east coast port can have an advantage over the other ports, based on government intervention and subsidization. For decades the complaint in the port of Halifax has been that the government policies favour the port of Montreal. I have nothing against the port of Montreal. I have nothing against appropriate and proper competition among ports. But I, like most people in Halifax, think that the port of Montreal is given advantages over the port of Halifax on the basis of government policy.
I could go back in history in other speeches I have made and detail those specific areas of advantage or disadvantage. Many years ago, the Government of Canada built substantial infrastructure within the port of Montreal. It gave the port of Montreal tremendous facilities at government cost, at taxpayers' expense, and then wrote off the debt. When the Government of Canada under the Liberals-and I do not blame my good friend from Newfoundland about that, those things
June 6, 1991

happen-wrote off the debts for the Canadian ports, the debt they wrote off for the port of Montreal was in the area of $600 million. The debt they wrote off for the port of Halifax was in the area of $100 million. I have the statistics. I presented them years ago to the House, but that is the kind of thing that has happened.
But the big gripe, the continuing gripe, the everyday gripe is the facilities that are made available to the port of Montreal for ice-breaking and navigation. Let me tell you as quickly as possible why that complaint exists.
Halifax is one of the greatest deep water ports in the world. You can get any kind of ship, any size of ship in. Mr. Speaker, as you are from Edmonton you may not be interested in this; you couldn't get a rowboat into Edmonton. In the port of Halifax any day of the week, any time of the day, you can get the largest ship in the world right up to the dock, no problem at all.
You cannot do that in the port of Saint John. I am not going to argue that point. But, in order to get that kind of vessel into the port of Montreal, you pretty nearly have to pick it up and carry it in. It is not quite that bad, but you have to have all kinds of navigational aids. You have to have all kinds of harbour dredging. You have to have all kinds of assistance, and you have to keep the shipping lane free of ice. Who does that for the port of Montreal? The taxpayers of Canada do it for the port of Montreal, because the Government of Canada provides that service and it is not charged to anybody. What we say in the Port of Halifax is: charge those services out to the users.
It is unbelievable from the perspective of Edmonton. For years the port of Halifax was saying: "charge those expenses out to the shippers, charge those expenses out to the users of the facilities". For years the Liberal government refused to do that. Finally, when the Conservative government came to power in 1984, it said that it was time to end this anomaly. It was time to end this unlevel field. It was time to create a proper atmosphere for competition.
The Government of Canada brought in Canada Shipping Act changes in Bill C-75. In that act there was placed a provision that would allow for services such as ice-breaking and navigation to be charged back to the users. The international shipping companies, from Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan, Europe, Hapag Lloyd from Hamburg-all those organizations-would have to pay the cost of ice-breaking, navigational aids and so on.
Government Orders
Do you know what happened? I do not want to embarrass the member from Newfoundland, but another member from Newfoundland, from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte, personally, individually stopped the passage of this legislation in this House of Commons by standing up for seven hours on third reading and stopping that legislation.
Do you know what he said in the House of Commons on October 31, 1986, which was more or less something he said earlier on June 27, 1986? He said that there was no way the Liberal Party was going to allow such a provision to be passed.
He said on June 27, 1986: "I think it is extremely important that the record be set straight, because we would not want the House to inadverently or accidentally get the impression that anyone in Canada is warped enough or misinformed enough to endorse clause 4 of Bill C-75".
Later, on another occasion, October 31,1986, he spoke of Bill C-75, clause 4, and he said: "That bill died on the vine because we in the Liberal Party opposed it". The Liberal Party opposed clause 4 of Bill C-74, which he said in his speech would allow the imposition of user fees. He said: "User fees for what?" User fees for Coast Guard service, navigational aids and ice-breaking services.
A member from Atlantic Canada stopped the legislative position that would have allowed for a level field between the port of Halifax and other east coast ports and the port of Montreal. It is on record; it is undeniable. Today, five years later and for the last 500 years since John Cabot or somebody sailed up some kind of strait, the port of Montreal has had an advantage over the port of Halifax. We can lay the blame on the Liberal Party of Canada.
They are still at it. They are still stopping measures that could be used to rebuild the competitive base, that could give the port certain advantage, that could provide for offsets to the At and East, that could get us on with the business of improving the port of Halifax.
Let me tell you what the most serious difficulty is now. It is inland transportation. It is the Canadian National Railway system. Unless the Canadian National Railway changes its attitude, unless it provides better facilities, unless we get better service through double stacking, rail

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
line improvements and lower rates, then we cannot be competitive.
People in the marine transportation industry are saying that if Halifax does not get competitive the port can die. It is almost impossible under the present situation for the port of Halifax to compete with the port of Montreal. Forget the port of Montreal. If was not them-and thank God it is-it would be the American ports. At least the business is staying in Canada. But in a short time it will be the American ports that are going to take all the business with the help of Canadian corporations like Canadian Pacific. They are buying railways and providing facilities that will allow Canadian destined cargo to go through American ports.
It is a very difficult situation. It will not be resolved unless we take the initial steps to correct the situation we now have: get rid of the subsidization that now exists, provide effective and constructive assistance , and get on with the matter of competition. There is in no other answer in international trade.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the hon. member for Halifax West and, first of all, I want to respond to the remarks he made about the member from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte.
The member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte did, as the hon. member just suggested, stand in the House of Commons for six or seven hours and spoke to the House. He dragged out the debate. He spoke all afternoon, all evening, and he was prepared to speak all night. In fact, I am sure he would have spoken for 48 hours or 72 hours if need be.
I want it on the record why the hon. member from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte stood here in the House of Commons last year and single-handedly filibustered a bill presented by the Government of Canada.
The hon. member who just spoke was absolutely correct. The member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte spoke against clause 4 of Bill C-75.1 do not recall exactly what the number was, but the clause had to do with imposing user fees for ice-breaker services in Canada.
I would like to put it on the record, in this way, why the member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte did what he did.
Today I had telephone calls in my office from two people who lived on an island called Long Island on the east coast of Newfoundland. One gentleman had to go to the doctor because he was having what he called radiation sickness. He was being treated for cancer. He was very sick and he felt very bad. He wanted to go from Beaumont, Long Island into Robert's Arm in Newfoundland to see the doctor there in order to be prescribed some pills because he was feeling so bad after he had taken the radiation treatment, which he told me he takes once a month in the Health Sciences Complex in St. John's.
He telephoned me, and his voice was not very good because the radiation had affected it. He said: "Look, I'm stuck here on this island and I cannot get in to see the doctor. The ice is all piled up around the shore and I cannot get in to see a doctor".
Now there are four islands in a row: Little Bay Islands that the hon. member for Labrador knows quite well; Long Island; then there is Change Islands further on; and then there is Fogo Island. Each one of those islands has ferry boats going back and forth, except right now the ice has clogged up everything. It goes out for about 180 miles.
This gentleman was saying: "Look, there is no helicopter service and planes cannot land". This is today, and he wanted to get in to see the doctor.
I checked with the Coast Guard and it said: "Well, we have one ice-breaker assigned to those four islands to try to keep it ice free. But we needed the ice-breaker today because there was a paper boat going into Beaumont and there was an oil boat that needed to go into Lewisporte and we only have one ice-breaker on all of that east coast of Newfoundland".
I phoned up the Coast Guard and I said: "Now, where are your ice-breakers? Don't you provide ice-breaker service anymore to these ferry boats along the coast?" It said: "Well, you know we have got a lot of business accumulated and we have got one ice-breaker on dry dock and we have another one with the propeller that was damaged". I said: "Well, where are all the other ice-breakers?" The Coast Guard said: "Well, there are seven sitting tied up to the dock in Quebec City."
June 6, 1991

I said: "Are those working?" The answer was: "No, no, those aren't working, but a couple of them are on stand-by. You see, we do not send anymore ice-breakers to accompany ships that go through the Arctic. We found that it is more cost-effective to leave the icebreaker in Quebec City tied up and if the ship gets stuck, we will send up the ice-breaker then-more cost effective".
There are another five tied up in Nova Scotia. I said to the Coast Guard: "Now, come on, you have islands that are being totally isolated because of ice. Can't you assign more ice-breakers to keep these islands open?" The answer was: "No, that is not the policy of the Coast Guard anymore. You see, we are into a policy of trying to save money".
See how things have changed. The hon. member a moment ago said: "The hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte stood in the House and he was opposed to user fees with ice-breakers".
Of course he was, of course he was. Why, if the Government of Canada brought in that policy there would not be any ferry boats operating. There would not be any because the ferry boats are no longer owned or subsidized by the Government of Canada. The Government of Canada did away with the subsidies for all those ferry boats, didn't they Mr. member for Labrador. He knows quite well. The government did away with that. Now it is whoever uses the ferry boats has to pay for them, not the Government of Canada.
In fact, when we think about this policy of subsidies and trying to save money we know quite a change has taken place in Atlantic Canada. The hon. member spoke about marine transportation, but that is only half the story. Marine Atlantic moves our freight and people throughout Atlantic Canada. Yet, Marine Atlantic has no 1-800 number anymore. We cannot pick up the phone anywhere in Canada and phone a 1-800 number to find out when the ferry boats are going to operate in Atlantic Canada. It was cut out this year by the Government of Canada.
We can no longer phone a 1-800 number to find out or make reservations on Marine Atlantic, but if we were in the United States we can.

That can't be true.
Mr. Baker Oh yes, oh yes. In other words, in Texas we can phone to find out when the ferries are operating. To
Government Orders
make a reservation to go to Newfoundland on a ferry or to P.E.I. phoning from Texas you can do it free of charge, but if you are living in Canada you cannot do it anymore. The Government of Canada through Marine Atlantic says it was because of the high costs that it wanted to keep the 1-800 number from the United States because fewer people were using the 1-800 number. Those are the decisions that have been made by the Government of Canada in trying to reduce subsidies for transportation in eastern Canada.
I was looking at the books the other day for marine transportation and I noticed that three vessels now used for the movement of freight on the east coast are not even registered in Canada. In fact, the last vessel that was hired by CN is actually not only registered in a foreign country, but owned in a foreign country.
Quite a change has taken place. If you picked up the telephone in that same area we are talking about, from Labrador down to the northeast coast of Newfoundland, you would no longer speak into the receiver of a company that is a subsidiary of the Government of Canada. That was sold last year.
Really?
Yes, and it was sold-this is a long story, but I am going to make it very short.
Oh, no, no, we want the story.

The successful bidder was the bigger telephone company in the province, represented of course by a consultant who happened to be yes, a former member of the House of Commons. That is the telephone company. We can no longer pick up the telephone and phone through a telephone company that was called TNT at the time, up until a couple of years ago-Terra Nova Tel.
That is an explosive.

It was an explosive telephone company. It was an excellent telephone company. You could phone and ask information what the number was for such and such and it would be able to tell you, because it was living locally in those areas.
The telephone company is gone. Now you go down to the airport. There is no longer a sign saying Air Canada. That is gone since this government took over. You can no longer pick up the telephone and phone through the government subsidized company, a subsidiary of the

June 6, 1991
Government Orders
Government of Canada that was making money every year. The government sold it.
There is no sign that says Air Canada anymore. Then there is the ultimate insult. In this bill we are talking about railway subsidies. We know what the government did to the railway. Every weekend when I am in my riding, I usually try to get a little bit of exercise and go for a walk. I go for a walk along where the railway line used to be.
That is pretty safe, eh, George.
Pretty safe. You will never get knocked down by a train because there is no track anymore.
You mean the government even took the track away?

It even took the track away. It not only took the trains away but took the track away. Not only that, but if you go a short distance to one of our smaller communities you will find a fellow who does not pick up the phone anymore through a government-run outfit to make a reservation on Air Canada, which is gone, or check on the train, which is no longer operating. Also, there is no post office in the community.
What. Oh, shame.

There is no post office in the community. Where is the federal identity at all in those communities? There is no federal presence at all. There is nothing. That is the policy of the Government of Canada.
What are we doing here today? Today we are dealing with a bill, Bill C-ll, that says that if you loaded flour on a railway car after July 15, 1989, and it has not arrived yet, then it is not going to be subsidized.
That is what the bill says. If you loaded the flour on the train after July 15, 1989, and it has not yet arrived, then it is not subsidized.
I just hope that it is not what they call bread and roll mix because those railway cars would have blown up by now. I do not know if there is any date on flour but maybe that is what I am doing wrong.
That is what the bill is. The bill is to do away with a subsidy that it did away with several years ago. The Government of Canada is not interested any more in paying a subsidy for anything going to the east coast of Canada.
Hon. members know today where the grain comes from for the livestock feed. Only 380,000 tonnes of it come from domestic places; 320,000 tonnes now come from the EEC or the United States. The government member stands up and says: "We've got to be in a competitive market. We've got to do away with all of these subsidies for moving grain and flour to eastern Canada". The most highly subsidized grain movements in the world are those in the EEC, which now exports grain to eastern Canadian markets and grain movements throughout the United States of America.
All in all, this bill is part of a general philosophy of the Government of Canada which says it is going to set people adrift. It is no longer going to be responsible for an even, fair and level playing field in Canada because it is going to say that those who have it will always have it and those who cannot afford it are never going to be able to get it.
Those people set adrift are the people in eastern Canada, the people in Atlantic Canada. It is the Government of Canada that is totally to blame.
I would suggest that the Government of Canada take a second look at this particular piece of legislation. I do not know what would happen if the bill did not pass. What would happen if the bill did not pass? Is there flour and grain aboard railway cars in Canada that has been there since July 15, 1989 waiting for export which was not completed until after January 31, 1990? What would be the legality? It is an interesting question.
If someone took the federal government to court and said: "Look, you are going to have to pay this subsidy because it is presently a part of the Railway Act and it was never amended by the Government of Canada", it would bring up the question of the supremacy of Parliament. Can the Government of Canada pass a bill which says it is going to discontinue a direct subsidy on a product from point A to point B without amending the legislation to end that subsidy? What would the judge say?
We all know the way legislation is treated. We have all appeared before judges on behalf of our constituents and we have presented arguments on everything under the sun. I have grave doubts whether the Government of Canada would be able to answer the question of why it discontinued a subsidy without amending the appropriate
June 6, 1991

legislation to end it. The Government of Canada should reinstate the subsidy and be true to its word.
